agentic-coding/03-algorithms/shell-sort.title: shell-sort
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/shell-sort.content:
Shell Sort

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
An improved insertion sort that first sorts elements far apart, then gradually reduces the gap. This pre-sorting makes the final insertion sort pass much faster.
📋 Concrete Example
Sort [5, 3, 8, 1, 4, 7] with gap 3: compare positions 0-3, 1-4, 2-5, swap if needed. Then gap 1 (normal insertion sort). The pre-sorting means fewer shifts in the final pass.
🔗 Analogy
Arranging books on a shelf by first roughly grouping them every 3rd book, then every 2nd, then adjacent. Each pass gets closer to sorted, so the final adjacent pass does very little work.
Related Concepts

Insertion Sort
Gap Sequence
Sorting
In-Place Sort

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/sliding-win.title: sliding-window
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/sliding-win.content:
Sliding Window

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
Maintain a window over a subarray and slide it efficiently, updating the result without recomputing from scratch. Great for range/substring problems.
📋 Concrete Example
Find max sum of 3 consecutive elements in [1, 4, 2, 10, 23]: window [1,4,2]=7, slide to [4,2,10]=16, slide to [2,10,23]=35. Max is 35. Each slide just adds and subtracts one element.
🔗 Analogy
Looking through a magnifying glass at a long scroll. You slide the glass along, and at each position you just update what you see rather than re-examining the whole scroll.
Related Concepts

Two Pointers
Array Technique
Subarray
Fixed Window
Variable Window

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/space-compl.title: space-complexity
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/space-compl.content:
Space Complexity

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
How much extra memory an algorithm needs as input grows. Sometimes you trade memory for speed, or vice versa.
📋 Concrete Example
An in-place sort uses O(1) extra memory — just a few variables. Merge sort uses O(n) extra memory for temporary arrays. A recursive algorithm uses O(depth) stack space.
🔗 Analogy
Packing for a trip. Minimalist packing (O(1) space) means washing clothes often (slower). Bringing many outfits (O(n) space) is faster but needs a bigger suitcase.
Related Concepts

Big-O Notation
Time Complexity
Auxiliary Space
In-Place Algorithm

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/stable-sort.title: stable-sort
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/stable-sort.content:
Stable Sort

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
A stable sort preserves the original order of equal elements. This matters when sorting by multiple criteria.
📋 Concrete Example
Sort students by score while keeping alphabetical order for tied scores. If Alice and Bob both score 90 and Alice was listed first, she stays first after sorting by score.
🔗 Analogy
Ranking runners by time, but for ties, the runner who registered earlier keeps the higher position. The sort respects the original order for equal times.
Related Concepts

Sorting
Merge Sort
Unstable Sort
Multi-Key Sort

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/streaming-a.title: streaming-algorithm
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/streaming-a.content:
Streaming Algorithm

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
Process a massive stream of data with limited memory, approximating results. You cannot store all the data, so you summarise on the fly.
📋 Concrete Example
Count distinct IP addresses in a web log with limited memory: use HyperLogLog to approximate the count using a few KB, even for billions of IPs.
🔗 Analogy
Counting different types of birds at a birdwatching spot. You cannot record every single bird (too many), so you use a tallying technique that approximates the diversity with a small notebook.
Related Concepts

Online Algorithm
Approximation
HyperLogLog
Limited Memory

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/string-matc.title: string-matching
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/string-matc.content:
String Matching

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
Finding a pattern string within a larger text. Naive approach is O(nm); smarter algorithms like KMP achieve O(n + m).
📋 Concrete Example
Find cat in concatenate: check positions 0 (no), 1 (no), 2 (no), 3 (yes! cat at index 3). Naive: check each starting position.
🔗 Analogy
Searching for a phrase in a book. The naive way: check every page position. Smart algorithms (KMP) skip ahead based on what they already know about the pattern.
Related Concepts

KMP Algorithm
Rabin-Karp Algorithm
Boyer-Moore Algorithm
Substring Search

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/strongly-co.title: strongly-connected-components
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/strongly-co.content:
Strongly Connected Components

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
In a directed graph, an SCC is a group of nodes where every node can reach every other node. Finding SCCs helps understand graph structure.
📋 Concrete Example
On a one-way road network, an SCC is a set of intersections where you can drive from any one to any other. Outside the SCC, you might not be able to return.
🔗 Analogy
A group of friends who can all message each other directly. Within the group, everyone can reach everyone. But someone outside the group might not be reachable by everyone inside.
Related Concepts

Directed Graph
Tarjan Algorithm
Kosaraju Algorithm
Graph Decomposition

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/sweep-line-.title: sweep-line-algorithm
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/sweep-line-.content:
Sweep Line Algorithm

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
Imagine a vertical line sweeping across the plane. Process events (points, intersections) as the line passes them. Used in geometry problems.
📋 Concrete Example
Find overlapping intervals: sort by start time, sweep from left to right, track active intervals. When a new interval starts before the previous ends, they overlap.
🔗 Analogy
A security guard walking along a corridor of doors. As they pass each door, they note who enters and exits. By the end, they know the maximum number of people in the corridor at any time.
Related Concepts

Computational Geometry
Event Processing
Interval Problem
Sorting

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/tabulation.title: tabulation
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/tabulation.content:
Tabulation

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
A bottom-up DP technique: build a table of solutions from the smallest subproblems up to the full problem, iteratively.
📋 Concrete Example
Fibonacci tabulation: table = [0, 1]; for i in range(2, n+1): table.append(table[i-1] + table[i-2]). Fill the table from small to large, no recursion.
🔗 Analogy
Building a multiplication table. You fill in 1x1, 1x2, 1x3… then 2x1, 2x2… Each entry is built from the ones before it. You work bottom-up.
Related Concepts

Dynamic Programming
Bottom-Up
Memoization
Iteration

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/tail-recurs.title: tail-recursion
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/tail-recurs.content:
Tail Recursion

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
When the recursive call is the very last operation, the compiler can optimise it to avoid growing the call stack. Some languages require this for deep recursion.
📋 Concrete Example
Tail-recursive factorial: def fact(n, acc=1): if n <= 1: return acc; return fact(n-1, n*acc). The multiplication happens before the call, so no stack frame is needed.
🔗 Analogy
A relay race where each runner passes the baton and immediately leaves the track. Only one runner is on the track at a time (no stack buildup), unlike regular recursion where all runners wait on the track.
Related Concepts

Recursion
Tail Call Optimization
Call Stack
Iterative Conversion

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/tarjan-algo.title: tarjan-algorithm
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/tarjan-algo.content:
Tarjan Algorithm

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
An efficient single-pass algorithm to find all SCCs in a directed graph using DFS and a low-link value. O(V + E).
📋 Concrete Example
Using DFS, Tarjan tracks the ‘discovery time’ and low-link (smallest reachable time) of each node. When a node’s low-link equals its own time, it is the root of an SCC.
🔗 Analogy
An inspector walking through a building who marks each room with an entry time. When they find a room whose earliest reachable room is itself, they know they have found a self-contained wing (SCC).
Related Concepts

Strongly Connected Components
DFS
Low-Link Value
Directed Graph

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/tim-sort.title: tim-sort
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/tim-sort.content:
Tim Sort

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
A hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort used by Python and Java. It detects already-sorted runs and merges them, making it extremely fast on real-world data.
📋 Concrete Example
Python’s sorted() uses Tim Sort. On data with existing order (like partially sorted lists), it runs in O(n) instead of O(n log n). It finds natural runs and merges them.
🔗 Analogy
A professional organiser tidying a messy room. They notice some shelves are already sorted (natural runs), leave those alone, and only merge and fix the disorganised parts. Much faster than sorting everything from scratch.
Related Concepts

Merge Sort
Insertion Sort

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/time-comple.title: time-complexity
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/time-comple.content:
Time Complexity

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
How the running time of an algorithm grows as the input size increases. This determines whether an algorithm is practical for large inputs.
📋 Concrete Example
A linear search through 100 items takes 100 steps. Through 1,000,000 items takes 1,000,000 steps. It scales as O(n). Binary search takes only about 20 steps for 1,000,000 items — O(log n).
🔗 Analogy
Time to find a book by scanning every shelf (O(n), linear) vs. using the catalogue to jump to the right shelf (O(log n), logarithmic). The catalogue scales far better as the library grows.
Related Concepts

Big-O Notation
Space Complexity
Worst Case
Best Case

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/top-down-dp.title: top-down-dp
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/top-down-dp.content:
Top-Down DP

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
Solving from the top (full problem) by recursively breaking it down and caching results. Natural to write but uses stack space.
📋 Concrete Example
Fibonacci top-down: fib(n) calls fib(n-1) and fib(n-2), caching each. You start from the big problem and work down to base cases.
🔗 Analogy
A manager who delegates tasks downward. They start with the big project, break it into sub-tasks, and assign each. If a sub-task was already done, they reuse the result.
Related Concepts

Dynamic Programming
Memoization
Recursion
Bottom-Up DP

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/topological.title: topological-sort
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/topological.content:
Topological Sort

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
Order the nodes of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) so that every edge goes from earlier to later. Essential for scheduling and dependency resolution.
📋 Concrete Example
Course prerequisites: CS101 -> CS201 -> CS301. A topological sort gives [CS101, CS201, CS301] — a valid order to take the courses.
🔗 Analogy
Getting dressed: underwear before trousers, trousers before shoes. A topological sort gives a valid dressing order where no item comes before its prerequisite.
Related Concepts

DAG
Directed Graph
Dependency Resolution
Kahn Algorithm
DFS Topological Sort

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/two-pointer.title: two-pointers
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/two-pointer.content:
Two Pointers

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
Use two indices moving through the array to solve problems like pair-finding, reversal, or partitioning in O(n) with O(1) space.
📋 Concrete Example
Find two numbers that sum to 10 in sorted [1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9]: left=0 (1), right=5 (9). 1+9=10! Or: left=1 (3), right=4 (7). 3+7=10!
🔗 Analogy
Two people walking toward each other from opposite ends of a corridor, checking items as they meet. Much faster than one person checking every pair.
Related Concepts

Array Technique
In-Place
Linear Time
Sliding Window

agentic-coding/03-algorithms/xor-trick.title: xor-trick
agentic-coding/03-algorithms/xor-trick.content:
XOR Trick

Domain: Algorithms

🎯 Motivation
XOR (^) has special properties: a^a=0, a^0=a, and it is commutative. This enables elegant solutions for finding unique elements and swapping.
📋 Concrete Example
Array [2, 3, 2, 4, 4]: XOR all -> 2^3^2^4^4 = (2^2)^(4^4)^3 = 0^0^3 = 3. The unique element is 3, found without extra memory.
🔗 Analogy
A game where matching cards cancel each other out. After pairing all duplicates, the one card left face-up is the unique one. XOR does this cancellation automatically.
Related Concepts

Bit Manipulation
Exclusive Or
Unique Element
Swap

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/api-g.title: api-gateway
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/api-g.content:
API Gateway

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A single entry point for multiple APIs. Handles routing, authentication, rate limiting.
📋 Concrete Example
Gateway: all API requests go to gateway.example.com. Gateway: authenticates, routes to User Service or Product Service, rate limits, logs. One entry point, many services behind it.
🔗 Analogy
An API gateway is like a building reception desk - all visitors enter through reception. Reception checks ID (authentication), directs to the right office (routing), and limits visitors per hour (rate limiting).
Related Concepts

Microservice
API
Load Balancing

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/bandw.title: bandwidth
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/bandw.content:
Bandwidth

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
How much data can be transferred per second. Higher bandwidth = faster downloads and uploads.
📋 Concrete Example
Bandwidth: 100 Mbps (megabits per second). A 1GB file takes 80 seconds to download. With 1 Gbps: 8 seconds. Higher bandwidth = faster data transfer.
🔗 Analogy
Bandwidth is like a highway’s width - a 2-lane road (low bandwidth) handles fewer cars. A 10-lane highway (high bandwidth) handles more cars simultaneously. More bandwidth = more data per second.
Related Concepts

Network
Latency
Throughput

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/cli-v.title: cli-vs-gui
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/cli-v.content:
CLI vs GUI

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
CLI (Command Line Interface) vs GUI (Graphical User Interface). CLI is faster for experts; GUI is easier for beginners.
📋 Concrete Example
CLI: ‘rm *.tmp’ deletes all temp files instantly. GUI: select each file, drag to trash. CLI is faster but requires knowing commands. GUI is intuitive but slower for repetitive tasks.
🔗 Analogy
CLI is like driving a manual car - more control, faster, but requires skill. GUI is like an automatic - easier to learn, but less control. Each has its place.
Related Concepts

Command Line
User Interface
Terminal

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/cloud.title: cloud-computing
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/cloud.content:
Cloud Computing

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Using remote servers over the internet instead of local machines. AWS, Google Cloud, Azure are cloud providers.
📋 Concrete Example
Cloud: you need 100 GPUs for AI training. Buy: 500,000. Rent from cloud: 10/hour x 100 = 1000/hour. Use for 10 hours, pay 10,000. Much cheaper for temporary needs.
🔗 Analogy
Cloud computing is like renting a hotel room instead of buying a house - you pay for what you use, when you use it. No maintenance, no upfront cost. But long-term, buying might be cheaper.
Related Concepts

Virtual Machine
Container
Scalability

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/comma.title: command-line
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/comma.content:
Command Line

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Using text commands instead of a graphical interface. Faster and more powerful for many tasks.
📋 Concrete Example
Command line: ‘grep error log.txt | sort | uniq -c’ finds, sorts, and counts errors in one line. With a GUI, this would take many clicks and tools.
🔗 Analogy
The command line is like giving direct orders to a butler - ‘bring tea, close the curtains, call a taxi.’ One sentence, multiple actions. The GUI would require finding each button.
Related Concepts

Terminal
Shell
CLI vs GUI

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/concu.title: concurrency
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/concu.content:
Concurrency

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Doing multiple things at the same time, but not necessarily simultaneously. Like juggling tasks.
📋 Concrete Example
A web server handles 100 requests concurrently: it starts request 1, while waiting for database, starts request 2, etc. Not simultaneous, but no idle time. Efficient.
🔗 Analogy
Concurrency is like a teacher monitoring multiple groups - they check Group A, then Group B, then Group C, cycling through. Not simultaneously, but all groups make progress.
Related Concepts

Thread
Parallelism
Asynchronous

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/conta.title: container
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/conta.content:
Container

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A lightweight, isolated environment for running applications. Shares the host OS kernel but has its own filesystem and dependencies.
📋 Concrete Example
Container: your Python app runs in isolation. It has its own Python version, libraries, and files. It cannot see other containers or the host. Lightweight because it shares the OS kernel.
🔗 Analogy
A container is like a private office in a shared building - you have your own desk, files, and supplies (filesystem, libraries). But you share the building infrastructure (OS kernel) with other offices (containers). Lightweight and isolated.
Related Concepts

Docker
Isolation
Microservice

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/cpu-c.title: cpu-core
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/cpu-c.content:
CPU Core

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A physical processing unit in the CPU. More cores = more parallel work. Modern CPUs have 4-16 cores.
📋 Concrete Example
4-core CPU: can run 4 threads simultaneously. 16-core: 16 threads. Your Python program can use multiprocessing to use all cores: 16x faster for CPU-intensive tasks.
🔗 Analogy
A CPU core is like a chef. 1 core = 1 chef. 16 cores = 16 chefs. More chefs = more dishes cooked simultaneously. But coordination overhead means it is not always perfectly 16x faster.
Related Concepts

Parallelism
CPU
Multiprocessing

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/cpu.title: cpu
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/cpu.content:
CPU

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
The CPU is the brain of the computer. It executes instructions: arithmetic, logic, input/output. Understanding CPUs helps you understand why code is fast or slow.
📋 Concrete Example
A 3GHz CPU executes 3 billion instructions per second. Your Python loop runs 1 million iterations: the CPU finishes in milliseconds. But if each iteration does complex I/O, it is slow because the CPU waits.
🔗 Analogy
The CPU is like a chef in a kitchen - they follow recipes (instructions), chop ingredients (arithmetic), check seasoning (logic), and plate dishes (output). A faster chef cooks faster, but they still need ingredients delivered (I/O).
Related Concepts

Memory
Operating System
Process

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/cuda.title: cuda
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/cuda.content:
CUDA

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
NVIDIA’s platform for running code on GPUs. Lets you write programs that execute on GPU cores.
📋 Concrete Example
CUDA: write C++ code that runs on the GPU. ‘Run this matrix multiplication on 10,000 GPU cores.’ 100x faster than CPU for large matrices. Essential for deep learning.
🔗 Analogy
CUDA is like giving instructions to 10,000 factory workers - you write one set of instructions (CUDA code), and all 10,000 workers (GPU cores) execute it simultaneously on different data.
Related Concepts

GPU
Parallelism
Deep Learning

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/devic.title: device-driver
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/devic.content:
Device Driver

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Software that lets the OS communicate with hardware: printers, GPUs, network cards. Each device needs its driver.
📋 Concrete Example
GPU driver: translates OS commands (draw this image) into GPU-specific instructions (NVIDIA RTX 6000 specific). Without the driver, the OS cannot use the GPU.
🔗 Analogy
A device driver is like a language interpreter - the OS speaks one language, the device speaks another. The driver translates between them so they can communicate.
Related Concepts

Kernel
Hardware
GPU

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/direc.title: directory
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/direc.content:
Directory

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A container for files and subdirectories. Also called a folder.
📋 Concrete Example
Directory: /home/user/ contains: documents/, photos/, music/ (subdirectories) and resume.pdf, notes.txt (files). Organizes files hierarchically.
🔗 Analogy
A directory is like a drawer in a filing cabinet - it holds folders (subdirectories) and documents (files). Nested directories are like folders within folders.
Related Concepts

File System
Path
File

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/dns.title: dns
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/dns.content:
DNS

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Domain Name System - translates human-readable names (google.com) to IP addresses (142.250.80.46).
📋 Concrete Example
DNS: you type google.com. DNS lookup: google.com -> 142.250.80.46. Your browser connects to that IP. Without DNS, you would need to memorize IP addresses.
🔗 Analogy
DNS is like a phonebook - you look up Alice and find her number 9876-5432. DNS looks up google.com and finds its IP address. You use names; DNS translates to numbers.
Related Concepts

Network
Internet
Domain Name

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/docke.title: docker
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/docke.content:
Docker

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Software that packages applications and their dependencies into containers. Runs identically anywhere.
📋 Concrete Example
Docker: package your Python app + all libraries + OS settings into a container. Run on your laptop, on a server, on the cloud - identical behavior. No ‘it works on my machine’ problems.
🔗 Analogy
Docker is like a shipping container - you pack your goods (app + dependencies) into a standard container. It fits on any ship, train, or truck (any machine). The contents are isolated and consistent.
Related Concepts

Container
Virtual Machine
Kubernetes

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/domai.title: domain-name
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/domai.content:
Domain Name

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A human-readable web address: google.com, cityu.edu.hk. Easier to remember than IP addresses.
📋 Concrete Example
Domain name: cityu.edu.hk. DNS translates it to an IP address. The browser connects to that IP. Domain names are human-friendly aliases for machine IP addresses.
🔗 Analogy
A domain name is like a person’s name - you say ‘call Alice’ instead of ‘call 9876-5432.’ Domain names are human-friendly labels for server IP addresses.
Related Concepts

DNS
URL
Internet

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/encry.title: encryption
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/encry.content:
Encryption

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Scrambling data so only authorized parties can read it. Used for security everywhere.
📋 Concrete Example
Encryption: Hello -> encrypted -> Xj7#kQ9m. Only someone with the key can decrypt it back to Hello. Without the key, it is gibberish.
🔗 Analogy
Encryption is like a secret code - you write ‘meet at noon’ as ‘zrrg ng abbA’. Only your friend with the codebook (key) can read it. Everyone else sees gibberish.
Related Concepts

TLS
Cryptography
Security

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/envir.title: environment-variable
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/envir.content:
Environment Variable

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Settings stored by the OS that programs can read. Used for configuration: paths, API keys, preferences.
📋 Concrete Example
Environment variable: PATH=/usr/bin:/usr/local/bin. Programs look here to find executables. API_KEY=abc123. Programs read this for authentication. No hardcoding secrets.
🔗 Analogy
Environment variables are like a student’s ID card settings - their name, student number, and access level are stored and checked everywhere. Programs check environment variables for configuration.
Related Concepts

Operating System
Configuration
PATH

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/event.title: event-driven-architecture
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/event.content:
Event-Driven Architecture

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Systems that respond to events: ‘user signed up,’ ‘payment received,’ ‘file uploaded.’ Each event triggers actions.
📋 Concrete Example
Event-driven: ‘user signed up’ event -> Email Service sends welcome, CRM Service creates contact, Analytics Service tracks. All triggered automatically by the event, not by direct calls.
🔗 Analogy
Event-driven architecture is like a fire alarm - when the alarm sounds (event), everyone knows what to do: call 999, evacuate, meet at assembly point. The event triggers automatic responses from multiple people.
Related Concepts

Pub-Sub
Microservice
Message Queue

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/execu.title: executable
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/execu.content:
Executable

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A file that can be run as a program. On Linux, needs execute permission. On Windows, has .exe extension.
📋 Concrete Example
Executable: python is at /usr/bin/python. It has execute permission. Type python in terminal -> OS finds it via PATH and runs it. The file contains machine code the CPU can execute.
🔗 Analogy
An executable is like a ready-to-eat meal - you do not need to cook it, just open and eat. The OS can run it directly. Source code (app.py) needs to be compiled or interpreted first.
Related Concepts

PATH
File Permission
Compilation

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/file-.title: file-permission
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/file-.content:
File Permission

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Who can read, write, or execute a file. Three levels: owner, group, everyone.
📋 Concrete Example
Permissions: rwxr-xr—. Owner: read/write/execute. Group: read/execute. Others: read only. ‘chmod +x script.sh’ adds execute permission for everyone.
🔗 Analogy
File permissions are like access levels in a school - the principal (owner) can enter any room, teachers (group) can enter classrooms, students (others) can only enter common areas.
Related Concepts

Executable
File System
chmod

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/file-.title: file-system
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/file-.content:
File System

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
How files are organized on storage: directories, files, permissions. The OS manages this.
📋 Concrete Example
File system: /home/user/documents/essay.txt. Directories (folders) contain files and subdirectories. Permissions: who can read, write, or execute each file.
🔗 Analogy
The file system is like a filing cabinet - drawers (directories) contain folders (subdirectories) which contain documents (files). Each document has permissions: who can read or edit it.
Related Concepts

Storage
Operating System
Directory

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/file.title: file
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/file.content:
File

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A named collection of data on storage. Can be text, image, code, or any data.
📋 Concrete Example
File: essay.txt contains 500 words of text. photo.jpg contains image data. app.py contains Python code. Each file has a name, type, and size.
🔗 Analogy
A file is like a document in a filing cabinet - it has a name (label), content (text or images), and a type (format). The file system stores and organizes files.
Related Concepts

Directory
File System
File Format

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/firew.title: firewall
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/firew.content:
Firewall

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Software or hardware that filters network traffic. Blocks unauthorized access, allows authorized traffic.
📋 Concrete Example
Firewall rules: allow HTTP (port 80), allow HTTPS (port 443), block everything else. An attacker trying to connect on port 22 (SSH) is blocked. The firewall protects the system.
🔗 Analogy
A firewall is like a security guard at a building entrance - they check each person (packet): ‘Are you on the list?’ If yes, enter. If no, blocked. Firewalls check network traffic against rules.
Related Concepts

Network
Security
Port

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/gil.title: gil
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/gil.content:
GIL

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Global Interpreter Lock (Python) - only one thread can execute Python bytecode at a time. Limits true threading parallelism.
📋 Concrete Example
Python GIL: even with 4 threads, only 1 runs at a time. Threads switch rapidly (concurrency), but not truly parallel. Solution: use multiprocessing instead of threading for CPU work.
🔗 Analogy
The GIL is like a single whiteboard in a classroom - only one student can write at a time. Others must wait their turn. Even with 4 students (threads), work is not truly simultaneous.
Related Concepts

Multiprocessing
Thread
Python

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/gpu.title: gpu
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/gpu.content:
GPU

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Graphics Processing Unit - designed for parallel computation. Thousands of cores. Used for AI training and gaming.
📋 Concrete Example
GPU: 10,000+ cores vs CPU’s 4-16. Each GPU core is simpler but there are thousands. Perfect for matrix multiplication (the core of neural networks). AI training uses GPUs because of this.
🔗 Analogy
A GPU is like 10,000 assistants doing simple tasks simultaneously - each one is not as smart as the chef (CPU), but together they chop 10,000 carrots at once. AI training needs exactly this: millions of simple calculations done in parallel.
Related Concepts

Hardware
Parallelism
CUDA

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/hardw.title: hardware
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/hardw.content:
Hardware

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Physical components: CPU, GPU, RAM, SSD, network card, keyboard, monitor. The tangible parts of a computer.
📋 Concrete Example
Hardware: you can touch it. CPU (processor), GPU (graphics), RAM (memory), SSD (storage), NIC (network). Software runs on hardware. Without hardware, software is just data.
🔗 Analogy
Hardware is like the kitchen equipment - stoves, ovens, refrigerators (CPU, GPU, RAM, SSD). Software is the recipes. You need both to cook: recipes without equipment are useless, equipment without recipes does nothing.
Related Concepts

CPU
GPU
Memory
Storage

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/http.title: http
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/http.content:
HTTP

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
HyperText Transfer Protocol - the protocol of the web. Browsers send HTTP requests, servers send HTTP responses.
📋 Concrete Example
HTTP request: ‘GET /api/users HTTP/1.1’. Response: ‘200 OK, Content-Type: application/json, Body: [{name: Alice}]’. Every web page load is an HTTP request-response.
🔗 Analogy
HTTP is like ordering at a restaurant - you (browser) say ‘I want the menu’ (GET /menu). The waiter (server) brings it. HTTP defines the format of these requests and responses.
Related Concepts

Protocol
HTTPS
REST API

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/https.title: https
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/https.content:
HTTPS

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
HTTP Secure - HTTP encrypted with TLS. Prevents eavesdropping. Used for all modern web traffic.
📋 Concrete Example
HTTPS: your request is encrypted before sending. Only the server can decrypt it. Someone listening on the network sees gibberish. Your password is safe.
🔗 Analogy
HTTPS is like sending a letter in a locked safe - only you and the recipient have the key. Anyone who intercepts it sees a locked box, not the letter. HTTPS encrypts web traffic.
Related Concepts

HTTP
TLS
Encryption

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/kerne.title: kernel
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/kerne.content:
Kernel

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
The core of the OS. Manages CPU, memory, devices, and system calls. The most privileged software.
📋 Concrete Example
Kernel: schedules processes, allocates memory, manages device drivers. When your program needs to read a file, it asks the kernel (system call). The kernel does the actual read.
🔗 Analogy
The kernel is like the building manager - they control electricity, water, elevators, and security. Residents (programs) request services through the manager, who handles the actual infrastructure.
Related Concepts

Operating System
System Call
Device Driver

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/kuber.title: kubernetes
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/kuber.content:
Kubernetes

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Orchestration platform for containers. Manages deployment, scaling, and operations of containerized applications.
📋 Concrete Example
Kubernetes: deploy 10 containers of your web app. Kubernetes: starts them, monitors health, restarts crashed ones, scales to 20 during peak traffic, scales to 5 at night. Automated container management.
🔗 Analogy
Kubernetes is like a fleet manager for delivery trucks - they decide how many trucks (containers) are needed, route them efficiently, replace broken ones, and add more during busy periods. Automated fleet management for containers.
Related Concepts

Docker
Container
Orchestration

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/laten.title: latency-in-networks
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/laten.content:
Latency in Networks

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
How long data takes to travel from source to destination. Lower latency = faster response.
📋 Concrete Example
Latency: Hong Kong to Tokyo server: 30ms (fast). Hong Kong to New York: 200ms (slower). Data travels at light speed through cables, but distance still matters.
🔗 Analogy
Latency is like travel time - a letter to your neighbor arrives in 1 minute (low latency). A letter to New York takes days (high latency). Network latency is travel time for data.
Related Concepts

Network
Bandwidth
Ping

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/load-.title: load-balancer
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/load-.content:
Load Balancer

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Distributes incoming requests across multiple servers. Prevents any single server from being overwhelmed.
📋 Concrete Example
Load balancer: 5 web servers. 1000 requests arrive. LB sends 200 to each. If server 3 crashes, LB sends its 200 to the other 4. Smooth, reliable service.
🔗 Analogy
A load balancer is like a traffic controller at a toll plaza - they direct cars to different toll booths (servers). If a booth closes, they redirect cars to open booths. No single booth is overwhelmed.
Related Concepts

Network
Scalability
Microservice

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/memor.title: memory
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/memor.content:
Memory

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Memory (RAM) stores data the CPU needs right now. Unlike disk, it is fast but volatile - data disappears when power is off.
📋 Concrete Example
Your program loads into RAM: variables, code, data. 8GB RAM means it can hold 8 billion bytes. If your program needs more, the OS uses virtual memory (disk), which is much slower.
🔗 Analogy
Memory is like a chef’s countertop - ingredients currently being used are on the counter (RAM). The pantry (disk) holds more, but walking to the pantry takes longer. Bigger counter = more ingredients at hand.
Related Concepts

CPU
Storage
Virtual Memory

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/messa.title: message-queue
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/messa.content:
Message Queue

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A system for asynchronous communication between services. Sender puts messages in a queue, receiver processes them later.
📋 Concrete Example
Queue: Order Service sends ‘process payment for order #123’ to the queue. Payment Service reads it and processes. If Payment Service is busy, the message waits in the queue. No data lost.
🔗 Analogy
A message queue is like a restaurant’s order ticket system - the waiter (sender) writes an order and puts it on the ticket rail (queue). The chef (receiver) picks it up when ready. The waiter does not need to wait; the order waits in the queue.
Related Concepts

Microservice
Asynchronous
Pub-Sub

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/micro.title: microservice
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/micro.content:
Microservice

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A small, independent service that does one thing well. Multiple microservices work together to form an application.
📋 Concrete Example
Microservices: User Service (login), Product Service (catalog), Order Service (checkout), Payment Service (billing). Each runs independently, communicates via APIs. One crashing does not bring down the others.
🔗 Analogy
Microservices are like departments in a school - Admissions handles enrollment, Finance handles fees, IT handles technology, Facilities handles buildings. Each department is independent. If IT is down, Admissions still works.
Related Concepts

Container
API
Monolith vs Microservice

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/monol.title: monolith-vs-microservice
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/monol.content:
Monolith vs Microservice

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Monolith: all code in one application. Microservice: split into small services. Each has trade-offs.
📋 Concrete Example
Monolith: one big Python app. Easy to develop, hard to scale. Microservices: 10 small services. Harder to manage, but each scales independently and one crash does not take down everything.
🔗 Analogy
A monolith is like a general store - everything in one shop. Easy to manage but hard to expand. Microservices are like a shopping mall - many specialized stores. Harder to manage but each can grow independently.
Related Concepts

Microservice
Architecture
Scalability

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/multi.title: multiprocessing
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/multi.content:
Multiprocessing

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Using multiple processes (not threads) for parallel work. Each process has its own memory. Avoids Python’s GIL.
📋 Concrete Example
Python multiprocessing: 4 processes, each with its own memory, running on 4 cores. True parallelism. Used for CPU-intensive tasks like data processing.
🔗 Analogy
Multiprocessing is like 4 separate kitchens - each has its own ingredients (memory) and chef. No sharing means no conflicts, but you cannot easily pass ingredients between kitchens.
Related Concepts

Parallelism
Process
GIL

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/netwo.title: network
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/netwo.content:
Network

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Computers connected to share data. The internet is a global network. Local networks (LAN) connect nearby computers.
📋 Concrete Example
Network: your laptop connects to a router (LAN). The router connects to the internet (WAN). You send a request to a server in Tokyo. Data travels through undersea cables in milliseconds.
🔗 Analogy
A network is like a postal system - your letter (data) goes from your house (laptop) to the post office (router) to the destination (server). The internet is a global postal system for data.
Related Concepts

Internet
TCP-IP
Client-Server

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/opera.title: operating-system
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/opera.content:
Operating System

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
The OS manages all hardware and software: CPU, memory, storage, processes. Windows, macOS, Linux are OSs.
📋 Concrete Example
OS jobs: schedule which process uses the CPU, allocate memory, manage files, handle network. When you run Python, the OS gives it CPU time and memory. When it crashes, the OS cleans up.
🔗 Analogy
The OS is like a school principal - they assign classrooms (memory), schedule teachers (CPU), manage supplies (storage), and handle emergencies (crashes). Everything runs through them.
Related Concepts

CPU
Memory
Process
Linux

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/orche.title: orchestration
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/orche.content:
Orchestration

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Automated management of multiple services: deployment, scaling, failover, load balancing.
📋 Concrete Example
Orchestration: 50 microservices running. Orchestrator: deploys updates one at a time (no downtime), scales busy services, restarts failed ones, balances traffic. All automated.
🔗 Analogy
Orchestration is like a symphony conductor - they coordinate all musicians (services), ensure timing, adjust volume, and handle mistakes. Orchestration coordinates multiple services for harmonious operation.
Related Concepts

Kubernetes
Microservice
Automation

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/paral.title: parallelism
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/paral.content:
Parallelism

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Doing multiple things simultaneously. Requires multiple CPU cores. True simultaneous execution.
📋 Concrete Example
4 CPU cores, 4 threads: each thread runs on a separate core simultaneously. 4 calculations done at the same time. True parallelism. 4x faster than 1 core.
🔗 Analogy
Parallelism is like 4 chefs cooking 4 dishes simultaneously in 4 kitchens. True simultaneous work. Concurrency is 1 chef switching between 4 dishes.
Related Concepts

Thread
Concurrency
CPU Core

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/path.title: path
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/path.content:
PATH

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
An environment variable listing directories where the OS looks for executable programs. Determines what commands work in the terminal.
📋 Concrete Example
PATH: /usr/bin:/usr/local/bin:/home/user/.local/bin. When you type python, the OS searches these directories for python. If found, it runs. If not: ‘command not found’.
🔗 Analogy
PATH is like a list of grocery stores you visit - you look for milk at Store A, then Store B, then Store C. The OS looks for programs in PATH directories, in order.
Related Concepts

Environment Variable
Terminal
Executable

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/port.title: port
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/port.content:
Port

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A numbered endpoint for network communication. Each service uses a specific port.
📋 Concrete Example
Ports: 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS), 22 (SSH), 5432 (PostgreSQL). A server listens on these ports. Clients connect to the right port for the right service.
🔗 Analogy
A port is like an apartment number in a building - the building (server) has many apartments (ports). You go to apartment 443 (HTTPS) for web, apartment 22 (SSH) for remote access.
Related Concepts

Network
Firewall
Socket

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/proce.title: process
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/proce.content:
Process

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A running program. The OS creates a process when you run a program, giving it memory and CPU time.
📋 Concrete Example
When you run ‘python app.py’, the OS creates a process: PID 1234, 100MB memory, 10% CPU. When the program finishes or crashes, the process ends and memory is freed.
🔗 Analogy
A process is like a student taking an exam - they get a desk (memory), time (CPU), and materials (files). When the exam is over, the desk is cleared for the next student.
Related Concepts

Operating System
Thread
PID

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/proto.title: protocol
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/proto.content:
Protocol

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A set of rules for communication. HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, WebSocket are protocols. Each defines how data is formatted and exchanged.
📋 Concrete Example
HTTP protocol: client sends ‘GET /index.html’. Server responds with ‘200 OK’ + HTML content. Both sides follow the HTTP rules. Different protocols for different needs.
🔗 Analogy
A protocol is like etiquette at a formal dinner - which fork to use first, how to address the host, when to start eating. Both sides know the rules, so everything goes smoothly. Network protocols ensure computers communicate correctly.
Related Concepts

TCP-IP
HTTP
API

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/pub-s.title: pub-sub
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/pub-s.content:
Pub-Sub

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Publish-Subscribe: publishers send messages, subscribers receive them. Decoupled communication.
📋 Concrete Example
Pub-Sub: User Service publishes user_created event. Email Service subscribes: sends welcome email. Analytics Service subscribes: tracks signup. Multiple subscribers, one publisher, no direct coupling.
🔗 Analogy
Pub-Sub is like a newspaper - the publisher (publisher) prints and distributes. Subscribers (subscribers) receive it. The publisher does not know who reads it. Multiple subscribers benefit from one publication.
Related Concepts

Message Queue
Microservice
Event-Driven

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/remot.title: remote-access
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/remot.content:
Remote Access

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Accessing a computer over a network. SSH, VNC, RDP are remote access methods.
📋 Concrete Example
Remote access: you are at home in Hong Kong, accessing a server in Tokyo. SSH gives you the command line. VNC gives you the desktop. You work as if you were there.
🔗 Analogy
Remote access is like a drone with a camera - you control it from far away, see what it sees, do what it does. Remote access lets you use a distant computer as if you were there.
Related Concepts

SSH
Network
Terminal

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/shell.title: shell
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/shell.content:
Shell

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
The program that interprets terminal commands. Bash, zsh, PowerShell are shells.
📋 Concrete Example
Shell (bash): you type ‘ls -la’. Bash interprets: list all files with details. It translates your commands into OS actions.
🔗 Analogy
The shell is like a translator between you and the OS - you speak human (commands), the shell translates to OS language (system calls), and translates the response back to you.
Related Concepts

Terminal
Bash
Command Line

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/socke.title: socket
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/socke.content:
Socket

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A communication endpoint: IP address + port. Programs use sockets to send and receive data.
📋 Concrete Example
Socket: 192.168.1.100:8080. Client connects to this socket. Server listens on this socket. Data flows through the socket. The connection is a socket pair (client + server).
🔗 Analogy
A socket is like a phone extension - you call the main number (IP), then dial the extension (port). The socket connects your phone to the right person. Sockets connect programs.
Related Concepts

Port
Network
TCP-IP

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/ssd.title: ssd
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/ssd.content:
SSD

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Solid State Drive - storage with no moving parts. Much faster than HDD. Uses flash memory.
📋 Concrete Example
SSD boot time: 10 seconds. HDD boot time: 60 seconds. SSD reads files instantly; HDD clicks and whirs. SSD is like a bookshelf - grab any book instantly. HDD is like a library - walk to the shelf.
🔗 Analogy
SSD is like a bookshelf where you can grab any book instantly. An HDD is like a vinyl record player - a needle physically moves to find data. No moving parts in SSD means faster access.
Related Concepts

Storage
Flash Memory
I/O

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/ssh.title: ssh
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/ssh.content:
SSH

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Secure Shell - a protocol for securely accessing a remote computer’s command line.
📋 Concrete Example
SSH: ‘ssh user@server.com’ from your laptop. You get the server’s terminal as if you were sitting in front of it. Encrypted, secure. Used for managing remote servers.
🔗 Analogy
SSH is like a remote control for a computer - you sit at home and control a server in a data center. You see its terminal, type commands, run programs. All encrypted so no one can eavesdrop.
Related Concepts

Terminal
Encryption
Remote Access

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/stora.title: storage
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/stora.content:
Storage

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Storage (SSD/HDD) keeps data permanently. SSDs are fast, HDDs are slow but cheap. Programs and files live here when not in use.
📋 Concrete Example
Your Python file is on SSD. When you run it, it is copied to RAM. When you save results, they go back to SSD. 512GB SSD holds 512 billion bytes - enough for millions of files.
🔗 Analogy
Storage is like a pantry - it holds all ingredients (files) permanently. The pantry is bigger than the counter (RAM), but getting something from the pantry takes longer than picking it up from the counter.
Related Concepts

Memory
File System
SSD

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/swap-.title: swap-space
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/swap-.content:
Swap Space

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Disk space used for virtual memory. When RAM is full, inactive data is swapped here.
📋 Concrete Example
Swap space: 8GB on SSD. When RAM fills up, the OS writes inactive memory pages to swap. Reading from swap is 100x slower than RAM, but it prevents crashes.
🔗 Analogy
Swap space is like an overflow storage room - when your desk (RAM) and backpack are full, you put items in the storage room (swap). Getting them back takes longer, but you do not lose anything.
Related Concepts

Virtual Memory
Memory
Storage

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/syste.title: system-call
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/syste.content:
System Call

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
How programs ask the OS to do things: read files, allocate memory, create processes. The program cannot do these directly.
📋 Concrete Example
System call: open(file.txt) -> OS opens the file and returns a handle. read(handle) -> OS reads data. write(handle, data) -> OS writes data. Programs request, OS executes.
🔗 Analogy
A system call is like ordering food at a restaurant - you (program) tell the waiter (OS) what you want, and the waiter brings it from the kitchen (hardware). You cannot go to the kitchen yourself.
Related Concepts

Kernel
Operating System
API

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/tcp-i.title: tcp-ip
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/tcp-i.content:
TCP-IP

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
The protocol suite that runs the internet. TCP ensures reliable delivery; IP routes packets to the right address.
📋 Concrete Example
TCP/IP: you send Hello to a server. TCP breaks it into packets, numbers them, sends them. IP routes each packet to the server. TCP reassembles them. If a packet is lost, TCP resends it. Reliable.
🔗 Analogy
TCP/IP is like the postal system - IP is the address system (where does this letter go?), TCP is the delivery guarantee (was it received? if not, resend). Together, they ensure reliable data delivery.
Related Concepts

Network
Internet
Protocol

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/termi.title: terminal
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/termi.content:
Terminal

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A text-based interface to the OS. You type commands, the OS executes them. Also called shell or command line.
📋 Concrete Example
Terminal: ls (list files). cd documents (change directory). python app.py (run program). git commit (version control). Text-based control of the computer.
🔗 Analogy
The terminal is like a walkie-talkie to the OS - you type commands, the OS does them and reports back. No mouse, no clicking - just text commands.
Related Concepts

Shell
Command Line
Operating System

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/threa.title: thread
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/threa.content:
Thread

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A unit of execution within a process. Multiple threads share memory. Enables concurrent work.
📋 Concrete Example
A web server process has 4 threads. Thread 1 handles user A, Thread 2 handles user B, etc. They share the same memory (same database connection). 4 users served simultaneously.
🔗 Analogy
A thread is like a worker in a kitchen - multiple workers share the same kitchen (memory) but each does a different task (chopping, cooking, plating). More workers = more dishes prepared simultaneously.
Related Concepts

Process
Concurrency
Parallelism

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/tls.title: tls
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/tls.content:
TLS

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Transport Layer Security - encrypts data between client and server. The S in HTTPS.
📋 Concrete Example
TLS: handshake -> agree on encryption keys -> all subsequent data is encrypted. Even if someone intercepts the data, they cannot read it without the keys.
🔗 Analogy
TLS is like a secret handshake between spies - they verify each other’s identity, agree on a code, then communicate in that code. TLS secures communication between client and server.
Related Concepts

HTTPS
Encryption
Certificate

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/url.title: url
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/url.content:
URL

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
Uniform Resource Locator - a web address. Contains protocol, domain, path, and parameters.
📋 Concrete Example
URL: example.com/articles/python Protocol: https. Domain: example.com. Path: /articles/python. Parameter: page=2. Everything needed to find a web resource.
🔗 Analogy
A URL is like a full postal address - protocol (delivery method: airmail), domain (city), path (street and building), parameter (apartment number). Everything needed to find a specific web resource.
Related Concepts

Domain Name
HTTP
Web API

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/virtu.title: virtual-machine
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/virtu.content:
Virtual Machine

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
A full virtual computer running on a physical computer. Has its own OS. Heavier than a container.
📋 Concrete Example
VM: a Windows VM running on a Mac. Full Windows OS, separate from macOS. 4GB RAM allocated. Heavier than a container (full OS) but fully isolated.
🔗 Analogy
A VM is like a house on a plot of land - it has its own foundation, walls, and utilities (full OS). Fully independent but takes more space and resources. A container is like an apartment - shares the building (OS) but has its own space.
Related Concepts

Docker
Container
Hypervisor

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/virtu.title: virtual-memory
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/virtu.content:
Virtual Memory

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
When RAM is full, the OS uses disk space as ‘virtual memory’. Much slower than RAM but prevents crashes.
📋 Concrete Example
8GB RAM full. OS moves inactive data to disk (swap space). RAM has space for active data. When the inactive data is needed again, it is moved back. Slow but prevents out-of-memory crashes.
🔗 Analogy
Virtual memory is like using a backpack when your desk is full - you put less-used books in the backpack (disk swap) and keep current books on the desk (RAM). When you need a backpack book, you swap it with a desk book. Slower, but you can work with more books than the desk can hold.
Related Concepts

Memory
Storage
Swap Space

agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/worki.title: working-directory
agentic-coding/04-computer-systems/worki.content:
Working Directory

Domain: Computer Systems

🎯 Motivation
The current directory your program is running in. Relative paths are resolved from here.
📋 Concrete Example
Working directory: /home/user/. Relative path ‘documents/essay.txt’ resolves to ‘/home/user/documents/essay.txt’. Change with cd in terminal or os.chdir() in Python.
🔗 Analogy
The working directory is like where you are standing in a building - relative directions (‘go to the room on the left’) depend on where you currently are. The working directory is your current position.
Related Concepts

Path
Directory
Terminal
