agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/a.title: agile
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/a.content:
Agile

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
An approach to software development: iterative, flexible, customer-focused. Deliver working software in short cycles.
📋 Concrete Example
Agile: 2-week sprints. Each sprint: plan -> build -> test -> demo -> reflect. Deliver a small, working feature every 2 weeks. Adapt based on feedback. Flexible, not rigid.
🔗 Analogy
Agile is like cooking a meal one course at a time - you make the appetizer, serve it, get feedback, then make the soup, adjust based on feedback, then the main course. You adapt as you go, rather than cooking everything at once and hoping for the best.
Related Concepts

Scrum
Sprint
Iterative Development

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/b.title: backlog
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/b.content:
Backlog

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A prioritized list of tasks, features, and bug fixes waiting to be worked on.
📋 Concrete Example
Backlog: 1) [HIGH] Fix login crash. 2) [HIGH] Add password reset. 3) [MED] Dark mode. 4) [LOW] Change button color. Prioritized by importance. Tasks are pulled from the top during sprint planning.
🔗 Analogy
A backlog is like a to-do list sorted by priority - the most urgent tasks at the top, nice-to-haves at the bottom. You work from the top down. The backlog keeps track of everything that needs to be done.
Related Concepts

Sprint Planning
Scrum
Task Prioritization

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/b.title: backward-compatibility
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/b.content:
Backward Compatibility

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
New versions should work with old code. Breaking compatibility forces all users to update.
📋 Concrete Example
Compatible: v2.0 can read files from v1.0. Users upgrade smoothly. Breaking: v2.0 cannot read v1.0 files. All users must convert. Avoid breaking compatibility unless necessary.
🔗 Analogy
Backward compatibility is like a new phone supporting old chargers - you can use your old charger (backward compatible) or you must buy a new one (breaking). Compatible upgrades are smooth; breaking ones are painful.
Related Concepts

Version Pinning
Dependency
Version Control

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/b.title: branch
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/b.content:
Branch

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A parallel line of development. You can experiment on a branch without affecting the main code.
📋 Concrete Example
Branch: ‘git checkout -b feature/dark-mode’. You are now on the dark-mode branch. Changes here do not affect main. When dark mode is ready, merge it into main. Safe experimentation.
🔗 Analogy
A branch is like a copy of a document - you edit the copy freely. If it turns out great, replace the original. If not, throw away the copy. The original is safe. Branches let developers experiment safely.
Related Concepts

Git
Merge
Pull Request

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/b.title: breakpoint
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/b.content:
Breakpoint

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A marker in code where execution pauses. Lets you inspect variables and step through code.
📋 Concrete Example
Breakpoint: set at line 10. Run code. It pauses at line 10. Inspect: x = 5, y = 3, result = 15 (wrong, should be 8). Step to line 11. result = 15 + 3 = 18. Found the bug: wrong calculation on line 10.
🔗 Analogy
A breakpoint is like a pause button on a video - you freeze the action at a specific frame and examine everything: ‘What is the score? Where are the players? What just happened?’ A breakpoint freezes code for inspection.
Related Concepts

Debugging
Debugger
Step Through

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/b.title: bug
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/b.content:
Bug

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
An error in code that causes wrong behavior. Bugs range from cosmetic to critical.
📋 Concrete Example
Bug: sort function returns [3, 1, 2] instead of [1, 2, 3]. The code has a bug. Debug: find the cause (wrong comparison), fix it, test. Bugs are inevitable; the goal is to find and fix them quickly.
🔗 Analogy
A bug is like a flat tire - it stops you from reaching your destination. You must find the hole (root cause), patch it (fix), and continue. Bugs are software flat tires.
Related Concepts

Debugging
Testing
Error Handling

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.title: clone
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.content:
Clone

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Making a local copy of a remote repository. You get all files and full history.
📋 Concrete Example
Clone: ‘git clone github.com/user/project.git’. You now have a full copy on your computer. You can edit, commit, and push changes back. Full local copy of the remote repo.
🔗 Analogy
Cloning is like borrowing a book from the library - you get a complete copy. You can read it, write notes, and when you return it, your notes are shared (push). You have the full book locally.
Related Concepts

Repository
Git
Push

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.title: code-review
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.content:
Code Review

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Having teammates review your code before it is merged. Catches bugs, improves quality, shares knowledge.
📋 Concrete Example
Code review: Bob reviews Alice’s PR. ‘Line 15: no error handling. Line 30: variable name is unclear. Line 45: good test coverage.’ Alice addresses feedback. Better code through peer review.
🔗 Analogy
Code review is like peer grading - a classmate reads your essay and gives feedback: ‘unclear thesis, great conclusion.’ You improve it before submitting. Code review improves code before merging.
Related Concepts

Pull Request
Code Quality
Collaboration

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.title: cohesion
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.content:
Cohesion

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
How focused a module is on one task. High cohesion = does one thing well. Good.
📋 Concrete Example
High cohesion: auth.py only does authentication - login, logout, token verification. Focused. Low cohesion: utils.py does authentication, database, formatting, and email. Unfocused. High cohesion is better.
🔗 Analogy
Cohesion is like a specialist doctor vs a generalist - a cardiologist (high cohesion) focuses on hearts. A general practitioner (low cohesion) handles everything. Specialists are better at their one thing. Modules should be specialists.
Related Concepts

Coupling
Modular Design
Single Responsibility

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.title: collaboration
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.content:
Collaboration

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Multiple people working on the same project. Version control, code review, and communication tools enable this.
📋 Concrete Example
Collaboration: Alice works on the frontend, Bob on the backend, Carol on tests. They use Git for version control, Slack for communication, GitHub for code review. Parallel work, combined results.
🔗 Analogy
Collaboration is like a group project - each person does their part, they communicate, combine their work, and review each other’s contributions. Software collaboration tools make this possible for code.
Related Concepts

Code Review
Version Control
Team Workflow

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.title: comment
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.content:
Comment

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Notes in code for humans. Explain why something is done, not what (the code shows what).
📋 Concrete Example
Good comment: ’# Use binary search because the list is sorted - O(log n) instead of O(n).’ Bad comment: ’# increment i by 1.’ The first explains why; the second is obvious from the code.
🔗 Analogy
A comment is like a margin note in a textbook - ‘This formula is used in physics.’ The note explains why, not what. The textbook (code) already shows what. Comments explain the reasoning behind the code.
Related Concepts

Docstring
Documentation
Code Readability

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.title: commit-message
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.content:
Commit Message

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A description of what a commit does. Good messages explain why, not just what.
📋 Concrete Example
Good: ‘Fix: sort function crashes on empty list. Added check for len(list) == 0.’ Bad: ‘fixed stuff.’ The message helps teammates (and future you) understand the change.
🔗 Analogy
A commit message is like a diary entry for your code - ‘Today I fixed the sort function because it crashed on empty lists.’ Future developers read these entries to understand why changes were made.
Related Concepts

Commit
Git
Documentation

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.title: commit
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.content:
Commit

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A saved snapshot of changes in Git. Each commit has a message describing what changed and why.
📋 Concrete Example
Commit: ‘git commit -m “Fix: handle empty list in sort function”’. This saves the change with a message. History: commit a1b2c3, ‘Fix: handle empty list in sort function’, Alice, 2025-08-01.
🔗 Analogy
A commit is like saving a video game - your progress is saved at this point. You can continue, and if you make a mistake, reload this save. Each commit is a save point for your code.
Related Concepts

Git
Version Control
Commit Message

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.title: coupling
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/c.content:
Coupling

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
How much modules depend on each other. Low coupling = modules are independent. Good.
📋 Concrete Example
Low coupling: auth.py and data.py communicate through a clear interface. Change data.py’s internals without affecting auth.py. High coupling: auth.py directly accesses data.py’s variables. Change one, break the other. Low coupling is better.
🔗 Analogy
Coupling is like the links in a chain - if each link is independent (low coupling), you can replace one without affecting others. If they are welded together (high coupling), you must replace the whole chain. Low coupling is more maintainable.
Related Concepts

Modular Design
Cohesion
Separation of Concerns

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/d.title: debugger
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/d.content:
Debugger

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A tool that lets you pause code, inspect variables, and step through execution. Essential for debugging.
📋 Concrete Example
Debugger (pdb in Python): set breakpoint, step line by line, inspect variables, evaluate expressions. ‘Why is x = 15 instead of 8?’ Step through to find where it went wrong. Far better than print statements.
🔗 Analogy
A debugger is like a slow-motion camera for code - you replay the execution frame by frame, seeing exactly what happens at each step. Where did the value change? Why? The debugger shows you.
Related Concepts

Breakpoint
Debugging
Step Through

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/d.title: debugging
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/d.content:
Debugging

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Finding and fixing bugs. Involves reproducing the bug, finding the cause, and fixing it.
📋 Concrete Example
Debugging: 1) Reproduce: run the code, see the wrong output. 2) Isolate: which function is wrong? 3) Inspect: add print statements or use a debugger. 4) Fix: change the code. 5) Test: verify the fix. 6) Check: did the fix break anything else?
🔗 Analogy
Debugging is like detective work - find the crime scene (bug), gather evidence (logs, state), identify the suspect (root cause), and fix the problem. Systematic investigation.
Related Concepts

Bug
Testing
Breakpoint

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/d.title: dependency
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/d.content:
Dependency

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
External code your project relies on. Libraries, frameworks, packages. Must be managed carefully.
📋 Concrete Example
Dependencies: requests (HTTP), flask (web), pytest (testing). Your code imports and uses them. If requests has a bug, your code has a bug. If requests updates and breaks compatibility, your code breaks.
🔗 Analogy
Dependencies are like subcontractors on a construction site - you rely on the electrician, plumber, and painter. If the electrician does bad work, your building has electrical problems. Dependencies are your code’s subcontractors.
Related Concepts

Dependency Management in Code
Requirements File
Version Pinning

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/d.title: docstring
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/d.content:
Docstring

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A documentation string inside code. Explains what a function does, its parameters, and return value.
📋 Concrete Example
Docstring: '''Calculate the average of a list of numbers. Args: numbers (list): List of numbers. Returns: float: The average. Raises: ValueError: If list is empty. ''' Right inside the code, above the function.
🔗 Analogy
A docstring is like a label on a kitchen spice jar - ‘Salt - for cooking, not baking soda.’ It tells you what it is and how to use it, right where you need it. Docstrings label functions in the code.
Related Concepts

Documentation
Comment
Code Quality

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/d.title: documentation
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/d.content:
Documentation

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Written guides for code: README, API docs, inline comments, tutorials. Essential for maintainability.
📋 Concrete Example
Documentation: README.md (project overview, setup, usage), API.md (endpoints, parameters, examples), docstrings (each function explained), CONTRIBUTING.md (how to contribute). Without docs, code is incomprehensible.
🔗 Analogy
Documentation is like a manual for a board game - without it, no one knows how to play. With it, anyone can learn. Code documentation is the manual for developers using or maintaining the code.
Related Concepts

README
Docstring
Code Quality

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/e.title: edge-case
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/e.content:
Edge Case

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Unusual or extreme inputs that might break the code: empty lists, zero, negative, very large, null.
📋 Concrete Example
Edge cases for sort(): empty list [], single item [5], all same [3, 3, 3], very large [1M items], null input, negative [-5, -1, -10]. The code must handle these correctly. Edge cases are where bugs hide.
🔗 Analogy
Edge cases are like extreme weather tests for a building - what happens in a typhoon? In an earthquake? In flooding? Normal conditions (common inputs) are easy; extreme conditions (edge cases) reveal weaknesses.
Related Concepts

Test Case
Unit Test
Robustness

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/e.title: end-to-end-test
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/e.content:
End-to-End Test

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Testing the entire application from user’s perspective: click button -> see result. Most realistic but slowest.
📋 Concrete Example
E2E test: 1) Open browser. 2) Navigate to login page. 3) Enter username and password. 4) Click login. 5) Verify dashboard appears. 6) Click Profile. 7) Verify profile page. Tests the real user experience.
🔗 Analogy
An E2E test is like a full preview performance - real audience, real stage, real lighting. Everything is tested as the audience (user) would experience it. Most realistic, but takes the most effort.
Related Concepts

Integration Test
Testing
User Experience

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/e.title: error-handling
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/e.content:
Error Handling

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Code that anticipates and handles errors gracefully: try/except, error messages, fallbacks.
📋 Concrete Example
Error handling: try: result = 10 / 0. except ZeroDivisionError: result = ‘Error: cannot divide by zero.’ The program does not crash; it handles the error gracefully. Better user experience.
🔗 Analogy
Error handling is like having a spare tire - if you get a flat (error), you do not abandon the car. You put on the spare (handle the error) and continue. Error handling lets programs survive problems.
Related Concepts

Bug
Exception
Graceful Degradation

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/e.title: exception
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/e.content:
Exception

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
An error that occurs during execution. In Python: ValueError, TypeError, ZeroDivisionError, etc.
📋 Concrete Example
Exception: int(abc) -> ValueError: invalid literal for int(). The code stops unless you handle it: try: int(abc) except ValueError: print(‘Please enter a number.’). Handled gracefully.
🔗 Analogy
An exception is like a fire alarm - something went wrong, and the program stops unless someone handles it. try/except is the fire drill: you know what to do when the alarm sounds.
Related Concepts

Error Handling
Bug
Try-Except

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/f.title: fallback
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/f.content:
Fallback

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A backup plan when the primary approach fails. Keeps the system running.
📋 Concrete Example
Fallback: primary AI model is down. Fallback to a simpler model. Fallback to cached response. Fallback to a default message. The system keeps responding, even if not perfectly.
🔗 Analogy
A fallback is like a spare key - if you lose your main key (primary fails), the spare key (fallback) gets you in. Not as convenient, but it works. Systems need fallbacks for reliability.
Related Concepts

Graceful Degradation
Error Handling
Robustness

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/g.title: git
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/g.content:
Git

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
The most popular version control system. Distributed: every developer has a full copy of the repository.
📋 Concrete Example
Git: ‘git init’ (start), ‘git add’ (stage changes), ‘git commit’ (save), ‘git push’ (upload), ‘git pull’ (download). Every change is tracked. Branches allow parallel work. Merges combine work.
🔗 Analogy
Git is like a sophisticated library system - every book (file) has a history of edits. You can see any past version. Multiple authors can work on different chapters (branches) and combine them (merge).
Related Concepts

Version Control
Repository
Branch

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/g.title: github
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/g.content:
GitHub

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A platform for hosting Git repositories online. Adds collaboration features: pull requests, issues, code review.
📋 Concrete Example
GitHub: push your repo. Others can: clone it, suggest changes (PRs), report bugs (issues), review code. Collaboration platform built on Git. Used by most open-source projects.
🔗 Analogy
GitHub is like a collaborative workspace - your project is there, and anyone you invite can view, suggest changes, discuss, and contribute. It is the office for code collaboration.
Related Concepts

Repository
Git
Pull Request

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/g.title: graceful-degradation
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/g.content:
Graceful Degradation

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
When something fails, the system continues to work with reduced functionality instead of crashing.
📋 Concrete Example
Graceful: API is down. Instead of crashing, the app shows cached data with a ‘Offline mode’ banner. Reduced functionality, but still usable. Better than a blank screen.
🔗 Analogy
Graceful degradation is like a restaurant running out of chicken - instead of closing, they offer beef and pork. Reduced menu, but still serving. The system degrades gracefully instead of failing completely.
Related Concepts

Error Handling
Robustness
Fallback

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/i.title: impact-vs-effort
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/i.content:
Impact vs Effort

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A framework for prioritization: high impact + low effort = do first. Low impact + high effort = skip.
📋 Concrete Example
Matrix: Fix login bug (high impact, low effort) = DO NOW. Rewrite architecture (high impact, high effort) = PLAN. Change font (low impact, low effort) = MAYBE. Add chat (low impact, high effort) = SKIP.
🔗 Analogy
Impact vs effort is like choosing which homework to do first - math assignment (high impact on grade, low effort) = do first. Rewrite notes (low impact, high effort) = skip. Maximize impact per effort.
Related Concepts

Task Prioritization
Backlog
ROI

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/i.title: integration-test
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/i.content:
Integration Test

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Testing how multiple components work together. Catches issues that unit tests miss.
📋 Concrete Example
Integration test: test_login_flow(): 1) Create user in database. 2) Send login request. 3) Check response token. 4) Use token to access protected page. Tests the full flow: database + API + authentication.
🔗 Analogy
An integration test is like a dress rehearsal with all actors - each actor (component) was checked individually (unit test), but now they perform together. Chemistry, timing, and flow are tested. Integration tests check the whole system.
Related Concepts

Testing
Unit Test
End-to-End Test

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/m.title: merge-conflict
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/m.content:
Merge Conflict

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
When two branches change the same code. Git cannot auto-merge. The developer must resolve it.
📋 Concrete Example
Conflict: Alice changed line 5 to ‘return a + b’. Bob changed line 5 to ‘return a * b’. Git: ‘CONFLICT on line 5.’ Developer must choose: addition or multiplication? Resolve and commit.
🔗 Analogy
A merge conflict is like two people editing the same sentence - Alice: ‘The sky is blue.’ Bob: ‘The sky is gray.’ You must decide: blue or gray? Someone has to choose. Git flags the conflict; the developer resolves it.
Related Concepts

Merge
Git
Branch

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/m.title: merge
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/m.content:
Merge

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Combining changes from one branch into another. Git automatically merges, or flags conflicts.
📋 Concrete Example
Merge: ‘git merge feature/dark-mode’ into main. Git combines the changes. If both branches changed the same line, conflict! Git asks you to resolve it. Otherwise, automatic merge.
🔗 Analogy
Merging is like combining two people’s edits on a group project - if Alice edited page 1 and Bob edited page 2, just combine them. If both edited page 3, line 5, you must decide which version to keep. Git does this for code.
Related Concepts

Branch
Git
Merge Conflict

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/m.title: modular-design
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/m.content:
Modular Design

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Breaking a system into independent modules. Each module does one thing well. Easier to build, test, and maintain.
📋 Concrete Example
Modules: auth.py (login), data.py (database), api.py (endpoints), utils.py (helpers). Each is independent, well-defined, and testable. Change auth.py without affecting data.py. Clean separation.
🔗 Analogy
Modular design is like a Lego city - each building (module) is separate. You can rebuild the police station without touching the hospital. Independent, interchangeable, maintainable.
Related Concepts

Architecture
Coupling
Separation of Concerns

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/m.title: mvc
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/m.content:
MVC

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Model-View-Controller - an architecture pattern. Model: data. View: UI. Controller: business logic.
📋 Concrete Example
MVC: Model: User database. View: login page. Controller: handles login request, checks model, returns view. Each part is separate. Change the view (redesign login page) without touching the model or controller.
🔗 Analogy
MVC is like a restaurant: Model (kitchen/ingredients), View (menu/dining area), Controller (waiter). The waiter takes orders, the kitchen prepares food, the dining area displays it. Each part is separate but works together.
Related Concepts

Separation of Concerns
Architecture
Design Pattern

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/p.title: pull-request
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/p.content:
Pull Request

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A request to merge your branch into the main code. Enables code review before merging.
📋 Concrete Example
PR: Alice opens ‘PR: Add dark mode feature.’ Team reviews the code: ‘Looks good, but add a test for the toggle button.’ Alice adds the test. Team approves. PR is merged. Code is reviewed before it goes live.
🔗 Analogy
A pull request is like submitting an article to a magazine - you write the article (branch), submit it (PR), the editor reviews it (code review), suggests changes, you revise, and when approved, it is published (merged).
Related Concepts

GitHub
Code Review
Merge

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/p.title: pull
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/p.content:
Pull

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Downloading the latest changes from a remote repository. Keeps your local copy up to date.
📋 Concrete Example
Pull: ‘git pull origin main’. Downloads Alice’s latest commits from GitHub. Your local code is now up to date with the remote. You have Alice’s changes.
🔗 Analogy
Pulling is like checking the class bulletin board - you read the latest announcements (commits) so you are up to date. If you do not pull, you miss your teammates’ changes.
Related Concepts

Git
Push
Fetch

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/p.title: push
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/p.content:
Push

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Uploading your local commits to a remote repository. Shares your changes with the team.
📋 Concrete Example
Push: ‘git push origin main’. Your local commits are uploaded to GitHub. Teammates can now pull them. Your changes are shared.
🔗 Analogy
Pushing is like submitting homework - you did the work locally (commit), now you submit it to the teacher (remote repo). The teacher and classmates can see your work.
Related Concepts

Git
Clone
Pull

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/r.title: readme
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/r.content:
README

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
The first file people read in a project. Explains what the project is, how to set it up, and how to use it.
📋 Concrete Example
README.md: ’# Todo App. A simple task manager built with React.  Setup. npm install. npm start.  Usage. Click Add to create a task.  Features. - Add, edit, delete tasks. - Categories. - Due dates.’
🔗 Analogy
A README is like a book’s back cover and first chapter - it tells you what the book is about and how to get started. Without it, people do not know what the project does or how to use it.
Related Concepts

Documentation
Repository
Project Overview

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/r.title: red-green-refactor
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/r.content:
Red-Green-Refactor

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
The TDD cycle: Red (test fails), Green (test passes), Refactor (improve code quality).
📋 Concrete Example
Cycle: 1) Red: write test, run, fail. 2) Green: write minimal code to pass, run, pass. 3) Refactor: improve code without breaking tests. Repeat. Each cycle adds one piece of functionality.
🔗 Analogy
Red-green-refactor is like sculpting - rough shape (red: test defines the goal), refine until it looks right (green: code works), then polish (refactor: clean up). Cycle by cycle, the sculpture (code) takes shape.
Related Concepts

Test-Driven Development
Testing
Refactoring

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/r.title: refactoring
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/r.content:
Refactoring

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Improving code structure without changing behavior - making it cleaner, faster, or more maintainable.
📋 Concrete Example
Before: 50-line function with nested ifs. After (refactored): 3 smaller functions, each 15 lines, clear names, same behavior. Easier to read and maintain. No new features, just better structure.
🔗 Analogy
Refactoring is like reorganizing your room - same furniture, same stuff, but better arranged. It functions the same but is more pleasant and efficient. Refactoring reorganizes code for better maintainability.
Related Concepts

Technical Debt
Code Quality
Code Smell

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/r.title: repository
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/r.content:
Repository

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A storage location for a project. Contains all files, history, and metadata. Often called a repo.
📋 Concrete Example
Repository: ‘my-project/’ contains: source code, tests, documentation, .git/ (history). Hosted on GitHub, GitLab, or local. The complete project with full history.
🔗 Analogy
A repository is like a project folder with a built-in time machine - it contains all current files and every past version. You can travel back to any point in the project’s history.
Related Concepts

Git
GitHub
Clone

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.title: scrum
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.content:
Scrum

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A specific Agile framework: sprints, daily standups, sprint planning, retrospectives.
📋 Concrete Example
Scrum: 2-week sprints. Daily 15-minute standup: ‘What did I do? What will I do? Any blockers?’ Sprint planning: choose tasks. Retrospective: what went well, what to improve. Structured Agile.
🔗 Analogy
Scrum is like a basketball team’s practice system - daily practice (standup), game plan (sprint planning), post-game analysis (retrospective). Structured, repetitive, focused on continuous improvement.
Related Concepts

Agile
Sprint
Standup

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.title: separation-of-concerns
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.content:
Separation of Concerns

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Different concerns (UI, business logic, data) should be in separate modules. Like MVC.
📋 Concrete Example
MVC: Model (data), View (UI), Controller (logic). Each concern is separate. Change the UI without touching data logic. Change the database without affecting the UI. Clean separation.
🔗 Analogy
Separation of concerns is like organizing a kitchen - raw ingredients (data), cooking (logic), and plating (UI) are in separate areas. Change the plating style without changing the recipe. Each concern is independent.
Related Concepts

Modular Design
Coupling
MVC

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.title: single-responsibility
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.content:
Single Responsibility

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Each module/class/function should do one thing. Easier to understand, test, and maintain.
📋 Concrete Example
Good: calculate_tax() only calculates tax. format_receipt() only formats. send_email() only sends. Each does one thing. Bad: process_order() calculates tax, formats receipt, sends email, and updates inventory. Too many responsibilities.
🔗 Analogy
Single responsibility is like a factory assembly line - each station does one thing: put on the wheels, paint the body, install the seats. Focused, efficient, replaceable. One thing per station (module).
Related Concepts

Cohesion
Modular Design
Separation of Concerns

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.title: software-engineering
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.content:
Software Engineering

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Writing one function is easy; building a large system is hard. Software engineering provides methods to design, build, test, and maintain complex software reliably.
📋 Concrete Example
A team of 10 developers building a banking app: they need architecture, version control, code review, testing, CI-CD, documentation. Without engineering practices, the project collapses into chaos.
🔗 Analogy
Software engineering is like city planning - building one house is simple, but planning a city requires zoning, infrastructure, traffic management, and building codes. Software engineering plans and builds large software systems.
Related Concepts

Version Control
Testing
CI-CD

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.title: sprint-planning
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.content:
Sprint Planning

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Choosing which tasks to work on in the next sprint. Based on priorities and capacity.
📋 Concrete Example
Planning: 10 tasks in the backlog. Team capacity: 6 tasks in 2 weeks. Choose the top 6 by priority. Assign owners. Sprint starts. Focused, realistic plan.
🔗 Analogy
Sprint planning is like planning a road trip - you have 10 destinations (tasks) but only 5 days (capacity). You pick the 5 best destinations and plan the route. Realistic, prioritized.
Related Concepts

Sprint
Scrum
Backlog

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.title: sprint
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.content:
Sprint

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A fixed period (usually 1-4 weeks) for completing a set of tasks. At the end, working software is delivered.
📋 Concrete Example
Sprint: 2 weeks. Tasks: implement login, write tests, fix 3 bugs. At the end: all done, demoed, deployed. Next sprint: new tasks. Predictable, iterative delivery.
🔗 Analogy
A sprint is like a study week before exams - you plan what to study, study intensively for a week, take the exams (demo), and then review what worked (retrospective). Focused, time-boxed effort.
Related Concepts

Scrum
Agile
Sprint Planning

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.title: standup
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.content:
Standup

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A short daily meeting: what did you do, what will you do, any blockers? Keeps the team aligned.
📋 Concrete Example
Standup (15 min): Alice: ‘Finished login UI, starting API integration, no blockers.’ Bob: ‘API is ready, need to write tests, blocked by missing test data.’ Quick, focused, action-oriented.
🔗 Analogy
A standup is like a hockey team’s quick huddle between periods - ‘I played defense, next I am on offense. Our goalie needs rest.’ Quick update, everyone aligned, back to work.
Related Concepts

Scrum
Sprint
Communication

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.title: step-through
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/s.content:
Step Through

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Executing code one line at a time in a debugger. See exactly what happens at each step.
📋 Concrete Example
Step through: line 1: x = 5. line 2: y = 3. line 3: result = x * y (result = 15). line 4: return result. You see: the bug is on line 3: it multiplies instead of adds. Found it by stepping.
🔗 Analogy
Stepping through is like replaying a video one frame at a time - you see exactly what happens in each frame (line). ‘Frame 3: the player kicks the ball.’ ‘Frame 4: the ball goes in the wrong direction.’ Stepping through reveals the exact moment things go wrong.
Related Concepts

Debugger
Breakpoint
Debugging

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.title: task-prioritization
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.content:
Task Prioritization

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Deciding which tasks are most important. Urgent vs important, impact vs effort.
📋 Concrete Example
Prioritization: Fix security bug (urgent + important) = do now. New feature (important, not urgent) = next sprint. Change button color (not important) = maybe never. Focus on high-impact tasks.
🔗 Analogy
Task prioritization is like triage in an emergency room - the most critical patients (urgent + important) are seen first. Minor issues wait. Prioritization ensures the most important work gets done first.
Related Concepts

Backlog
Scrum
Impact vs Effort

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.title: team-workflow
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.content:
Team Workflow

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
How a team organizes work: who does what, how changes are reviewed, how releases happen.
📋 Concrete Example
Workflow: 1) Pick a task from the board. 2) Create a branch. 3) Code. 4) Write tests. 5) Open PR. 6) Code review. 7) Merge. 8) Deploy. Structured, repeatable process.
🔗 Analogy
A team workflow is like a kitchen brigade system - the head chef assigns tasks, each cook prepares their dish, the sous-chef checks quality, and the expediter sends orders out. Everyone has a role; the process is structured.
Related Concepts

Collaboration
Agile
Scrum

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.title: technical-debt
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.content:
Technical Debt

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Quick-and-dirty code saves time now but creates debt that must be paid back later with interest (harder maintenance).
📋 Concrete Example
Rushing: copy-paste code 5 times (fast now). Debt: when you need to change the logic, you must change 5 places (slow later). The model can identify and help pay down debt.
🔗 Analogy
Technical debt is like using a credit card - buy now (fast), pay later with interest (expensive). Quick code is like credit card debt: convenient now, costly later. Pay it down by refactoring.
Related Concepts

Refactoring
Code Quality
Code Smell

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.title: test-case
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.content:
Test Case

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
A specific scenario to test: input + expected output. Many test cases cover different scenarios.
📋 Concrete Example
Test cases for sort(): 1) Empty list -> []. 2) One item -> same. 3) Sorted list -> same. 4) Reverse sorted -> sorted. 5) Duplicates -> sorted. 6) Negative numbers -> sorted. 7) Large list -> sorted. Each case checks a scenario.
🔗 Analogy
A test case is like a specific exam question - ‘Solve x + 5 = 10.’ One question, one expected answer. Many questions (test cases) cover the full topic. Each case checks one specific scenario.
Related Concepts

Unit Test
Testing
Edge Case

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.title: test-driven-development
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.content:
Test-Driven Development

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Write tests before code. Red (test fails) -> Green (code passes) -> Refactor (improve). TDD cycle.
📋 Concrete Example
TDD: 1) Write test: assert is_prime(7) == True. 2) Run: FAIL (function does not exist). Red. 3) Write code: def is_prime(n): return True. 4) Run: PASS. Green. 5) Write more tests, fix code. Cycle.
🔗 Analogy
TDD is like writing the exam before studying - you write the test (what should the code do?), then learn (write code) until you pass. It ensures you know the goal before you start coding.
Related Concepts

Testing
Unit Test
Red-Green-Refactor

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.title: testing
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.content:
Testing

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Verifying that code works correctly. Unit tests, integration tests, end-to-end tests. Essential for quality.
📋 Concrete Example
Testing: write test_add(): assert add(2, 3)  5. Run it. Pass! Now test edge cases: assert add(0, 0)  0, assert add(-1, 1) == 0. Each test verifies a specific behavior. Catches bugs early.
🔗 Analogy
Testing is like a dress rehearsal before a play - you practice everything to find problems before the real performance (production). Each test checks one aspect. Finding bugs in rehearsal is better than during the show.
Related Concepts

Unit Test
Integration Test
Test Coverage

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.title: try-except
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/t.content:
Try-Except

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Python’s error handling: try something, except catch the error. Prevents crashes.
📋 Concrete Example
try: file = open(data.txt) except FileNotFoundError: print(‘File not found. Creating a new one.’) file = open(data.txt, w). The error is caught and handled. No crash.
🔗 Analogy
try-except is like wearing a seatbelt - you try to drive safely, but if something goes wrong (exception), the seatbelt (except) protects you. The program survives the error.
Related Concepts

Exception
Error Handling
Python

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/u.title: unit-test
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/u.content:
Unit Test

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Testing the smallest unit of code (a function) in isolation. Fast, specific, numerous.
📋 Concrete Example
Unit test: test_sort_empty_list(): assert sort([])  []. test_sort_one_item(): assert sort([5])  [5]. test_sort_duplicates(): assert sort([3, 1, 3]) == [1, 3, 3]. Each function tested separately.
🔗 Analogy
A unit test is like checking each ingredient before cooking - is the egg fresh? Is the flour dry? Each ingredient (function) is checked individually. If all pass, the dish (program) has a good foundation.
Related Concepts

Testing
Test Coverage
Test Case

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/v.title: version-control
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/v.content:
Version Control

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Tracking changes to code over time. Who changed what, when, and why. Essential for team collaboration.
📋 Concrete Example
Git: Alice changes line 10. Bob changes line 20. Both commit. Git merges the changes. History: ‘Alice: fixed login bug, 2025-08-01 14:00.’ Full traceability. Rollback if needed.
🔗 Analogy
Version control is like a time machine for your code - you can see what the code looked like at any point in history, who made each change, and why. If something breaks, you can go back in time.
Related Concepts

Git
Commit
Branch

agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/v.title: version-pinning
agentic-coding/06-software-engineering/v.content:
Version Pinning

Domain: Software Engineering

🎯 Motivation
Specifying exact versions of dependencies to prevent unexpected breaks.
📋 Concrete Example
Pin: ‘requests==2.31.0’ (exactly this version). If requests releases 2.32 with breaking changes, your code is safe. You upgrade deliberately, not accidentally.
🔗 Analogy
Version pinning is like locking in a flight price - you pay exactly the price you saw. If prices go up, you are not affected. Pinning locks dependency versions to prevent unexpected breaks.
Related Concepts

Dependency
Requirements File
Backward Compatibility

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/activa.title: activation-function
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/activa.content:
Activation Function

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
Adds non-linearity so the network can learn complex patterns, not just straight-line rules.
📋 Concrete Example
ReLU turns negative inputs to zero and keeps positives. Sigmoid squashes values to between 0 and 1.
🔗 Analogy
Like a gate that only opens if you push hard enough - without it, the network would only draw straight lines.
Related Concepts

ReLU
Sigmoid
Tanh
Neuron
Non-Linearity

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/ai-vs-.title: ai-vs-ml-vs-dl
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/ai-vs-.content:
AI vs ML vs DL

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
Computers can do smart things in different ways. Knowing the difference helps you pick the right tool.
📋 Concrete Example
AI is the big umbrella (any program that seems smart). ML is a subset where the program learns from data. DL is a subset of ML using neural networks with many layers.
🔗 Analogy
AI is like cooking food in general. ML is cooking by tasting and adjusting. DL is cooking with a fancy multi-layer oven that learns recipes itself.
Related Concepts

Supervised Learning
Unsupervised Learning
Neural Network

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/attent.title: attention
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/attent.content:
Attention

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
Lets the model focus on the most relevant parts of the input when making each prediction.
📋 Concrete Example
Translating the bank of the river, attention links bank to river not to money-bank.
🔗 Analogy
Like a student skimming a long article and highlighting only the sentences relevant to the question.
Related Concepts

Self-Attention
Transformer Architecture
Embedding

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/backpr.title: backpropagation
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/backpr.content:
Backpropagation

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
Calculates how much each weight contributed to the error, so we can adjust them. The learning step.
📋 Concrete Example
The model predicted cat with 60% but the true label is dog. Backprop computes gradients telling each weight how to change.
🔗 Analogy
Like a coach reviewing a lost game with each player, telling them exactly what to fix for next time.
Related Concepts

Forward Pass
Gradient Descent
Loss Function
Chain Rule

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/batch.title: batch
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/batch.content:
Batch

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
A small chunk of data processed before updating weights. Makes training faster and more stable.
📋 Concrete Example
With 1000 images and batch size 50, each batch has 50 images, giving 20 updates per epoch.
🔗 Analogy
Like eating a big meal in small bites instead of all at once - easier to digest.
Related Concepts

Epoch
Mini-Batch Gradient Descent
Training

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/biases.title: biases
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/biases.content:
Biases

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
A bias shifts the neuron output so it can fire even when inputs are zero, giving the model flexibility.
📋 Concrete Example
A neuron with bias = -2 will not fire easily. Changing bias to +3 makes it fire more often for the same inputs.
🔗 Analogy
Like a thermostat offset - even if the room temperature reading is the same, you can nudge the system to heat earlier.
Related Concepts

Weights
Neuron
Activation Function

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/classi.title: classification
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/classi.content:
Classification

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
Predicting a category label from a fixed set of options.
📋 Concrete Example
Given an email, predict spam or not spam. Given a photo, predict which of 10 animals.
🔗 Analogy
Like sorting mail into labeled bins - each item goes into exactly one category.
Related Concepts

Regression
Softmax
Cross-Entropy Loss
Supervised Learning

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/cluste.title: clustering
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/cluste.content:
Clustering

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
Grouping similar items together without labels. A key unsupervised task.
📋 Concrete Example
Group shoppers by buying habits into clusters like weekly groceries, luxury, impulse buyers.
🔗 Analogy
Like organizing a big box of mixed buttons into piles by color and size, with no labels given.
Related Concepts

Unsupervised Learning
K-Means
Dimensionality Reduction

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/cross-.title: cross-entropy-loss
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/cross-.content:
Cross-Entropy Loss

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
A loss function for classification that rewards confident correct predictions and punishes wrong confident ones.
📋 Concrete Example
If the model says 0.9 probability for the correct class, loss is small. If it says 0.1, loss is large.
🔗 Analogy
Like an exam that gives full marks only if you are both correct and confident - guessing right by luck gives little credit.
Related Concepts

Loss Function
Softmax
Classification
Entropy

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/datase.title: dataset
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/datase.content:
Dataset

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
The collection of examples used to train and test a model. Bigger and cleaner is usually better.
📋 Concrete Example
ImageNet is a dataset with over 14 million labeled images across 1000 categories.
🔗 Analogy
Like a library - the bigger and better organized it is, the more you can learn from it.
Related Concepts

Train Validation Test Split
Feature
Label

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/deep-l.title: deep-learning
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/deep-l.content:
Deep Learning

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
Machine learning using neural networks with many layers. Deep means many layers.
📋 Concrete Example
A 50-layer network classifying medical X-rays is deep learning. A 2-layer network is shallow.
🔗 Analogy
Like a multi-story factory: the more floors (layers), the more complex the product it can make.
Related Concepts

Neural Network
Layers
Backpropagation

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/dimens.title: dimensionality-reduction
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/dimens.content:
Dimensionality Reduction

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
Squeezing data with many features into fewer dimensions while keeping the important info.
📋 Concrete Example
Reduce 1000-pixel images to a 50-number summary that still captures the key shapes.
🔗 Analogy
Like summarizing a 300-page book into a 1-page synopsis that keeps the main plot.
Related Concepts

PCA
Embedding
Clustering

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/dropou.title: dropout
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/dropou.content:
Dropout

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
Randomly turns off some neurons during training so the network does not rely too much on any one path.
📋 Concrete Example
During each training step, 20% of neurons are randomly dropped. At inference, all neurons are used.
🔗 Analogy
Like a sports coach benching random players during practice so the team learns to work together, not depend on one star.
Related Concepts

Regularization
Overfitting
Neural Network

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/embedd.title: embedding
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/embedd.content:
Embedding

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
Turning things like words or images into lists of numbers so a computer can compare them.
📋 Concrete Example
The word king might become [0.5, -0.2, 0.9, …]. Similar words like queen get similar vectors.
🔗 Analogy
Like giving each student a ID badge with numbers - students with similar interests get similar numbers.
Related Concepts

Word2Vec
Dimensionality Reduction
Feature

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/epoch.title: epoch
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/epoch.content:
Epoch

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
One full pass through the entire training dataset. Training runs for many epochs.
📋 Concrete Example
With 1000 images and batch size 100, one epoch = 10 batches = 10 weight updates.
🔗 Analogy
Like reading a textbook cover to cover once. You read it many times to really learn it.
Related Concepts

Batch
Training
Iteration

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/featur.title: feature-engineering
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/featur.content:
Feature Engineering

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
Creating useful new features from raw data to help the model learn better.
📋 Concrete Example
From date of birth, engineer an age feature. From address, engineer distance-to-MTR feature.
🔗 Analogy
Like a chef prepping ingredients before cooking - cutting and seasoning well makes the dish better.
Related Concepts

Feature
Dataset
Training

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/featur.title: feature
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/featur.content:
Feature

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
An individual measurable property used as input. Good features make learning easier.
📋 Concrete Example
For predicting house price, features might be area, number of rooms, age, and location.
🔗 Analogy
Like the clues a detective collects - each clue (feature) helps solve the case.
Related Concepts

Label
Dataset
Feature Engineering

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/fine-t.title: fine-tuning
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/fine-t.content:
Fine-Tuning

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation

Pushing input through the network to get a prediction. The everyday use of a trained model.

How well a model performs on new unseen data, not just the data it trained on.

A model that gets 99% on training data but only 60% on test data generalizes poorly.

Adjusts weights step by step downhill on the loss surface to reduce error.

If the loss goes down when you increase weight A, gradient descent increases weight A a little. Repeat.

Layers between input and output where the network learns internal representations.

🎯 Motivation
Settings chosen by the human before training, not learned from data.

Learning rate, number of layers, batch size, and number of epochs are hyperparameters you set before training starts.

🎯 Motivation
Using a trained model to make predictions on new, unseen data.

🎯 Motivation
Receives the raw data, one neuron per feature. No computation - just passes values in.

Like the front desk of a company - it receives visitors (data) and routes them inside.

K-Means

🎯 Motivation
A clustering algorithm that assigns each point to the nearest of K centers, then updates centers.
📋 Concrete Example
K-means on customer data with K=3 finds three customer types based on spending patterns.
🔗 Analogy
Like choosing 3 meeting points in a city and asking everyone to go to the nearest one, then re-centering.

Clustering
Unsupervised Learning

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/l1-l2-.content:
L1 L2 Regularization

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
L1 adds a penalty based on absolute weight values (can zero out weights). L2 adds a penalty based on squared weights.
📋 Concrete Example
L1 can shrink unimportant weights to exactly zero, doing feature selection. L2 keeps all weights small but nonzero.
🔗 Analogy
L1 is like a strict editor who deletes whole paragraphs. L2 is like one who trims every word a little.

Regularization
Overfitting
Weights

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/label.title: label
agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/label.content:
Label

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
The correct answer paired with input features in supervised learning.
📋 Concrete Example
In a spam dataset, each email (features) has a label: spam or not spam.
🔗 Analogy
Like the answer key next to each practice question - tells the model what to aim for.

Feature
Supervised Learning
Dataset

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/layers.content:
Layers

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
A neural network is built from stacked layers, each transforming the data step by step.
📋 Concrete Example
A cat classifier might have an input layer (pixels), 3 hidden layers (features), and an output layer (cat or dog).

Like a relay race: each runner (layer) takes the baton (data), transforms it, and hands it to the next runner.

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/learni.content:
Learning Rate

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
Controls how big each weight update step is. Too big diverges, too small is slow.
📋 Concrete Example
Learning rate 0.001 means each step changes weights by a tiny amount. 0.5 might overshoot and explode.
🔗 Analogy
Like adjusting a shower tap: tiny turns find the right temperature; big turns scald or freeze you.

Gradient Descent
Hyperparameters
Training

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/loss-f.content:
Loss Function

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
Measures how wrong the predictions are. Training tries to make this number as small as possible.
📋 Concrete Example
Mean squared error: average of (prediction - true value) squared across examples.
🔗 Analogy
Like a scoreboard that shows your mistakes - the lower the score, the better you are doing.

agentic-coding/07-ai-fundamentals/mean-s.content:
Mean Squared Error

Domain: AI Fundamentals

🎯 Motivation
A loss function for regression: average of squared differences between predictions and true values.
📋 Concrete Example
Predict house price 4.2M, actual 4.0M. Error = 0.2M. Squared = 0.04. Average over all houses gives MSE.

Like measuring how far your darts land from the bullseye, squaring the distances so big misses hurt more.

Regression
Variance

🎯 Motivation
Update weights using small batches of data - a balance between speed and stability.
📋 Concrete Example
Batch size 32: each update uses 32 examples. Faster than full-batch, smoother than one-at-a-time.

Like a teacher grading 32 papers at a time to estimate the class average, instead of all at once or one by one.

🎯 Motivation
How complex a pattern the model can learn. More parameters usually means higher capacity.

A linear model has low capacity (straight lines only). A 100-layer network has very high capacity.

A model inspired by the brain that can learn very complex patterns when given enough data.

A network with layers of connected neurons takes pixel values of a photo and outputs the probability it is a cat.

The basic unit of a neural network. It combines inputs and decides how much signal to pass forward.

A neuron takes 3 numbers, multiplies each by a weight, adds a bias, then applies ReLU. Output goes to the next layer.

The ability to model curved, complex relationships, not just straight lines. Comes from activation functions.

Without non-linearity, a 100-layer network collapses to the equivalent of one linear layer.

The final layer that produces the prediction or decision.

The model memorizes training data including noise, so it fails on new data.

A student memorizes past-paper answers word for word but cannot solve a slightly different exam question.

The numbers inside the model (weights and biases) that get learned from data.

Principal Component Analysis finds the directions of most variance and projects data onto them.

The simplest neural unit - a single neuron that makes a yes/no decision. The ancestor of modern networks.

A perceptron takes exam score and homework score, multiplies by weights, and outputs pass or fail.

In reinforcement learning, the strategy the agent uses to choose actions based on the current state.

Training a model on a huge general dataset before fine-tuning on a specific task.

Techniques that prevent overfitting by keeping the model simple or robust.

An agent learns by trying actions and getting rewards or penalties, improving over time.

Squashes any number into the range 0 to 1, useful for probabilities and binary outputs.

Sigmoid(0) = 0.5, Sigmoid(10) is about 0.99995, Sigmoid(-10) is about 0.00005.

Turns a list of numbers into probabilities that sum to 1. Used in classification output layers.

Raw scores [2.0, 1.0, 0.1] become probabilities [0.7, 0.2, 0.1] after softmax.

Reuse knowledge learned on one task to help learn another task faster and better.

Chain Rule

🎯 Motivation
Updates our belief when we see new evidence. The backbone of many reasoning systems.
📋 Concrete Example
If 1% of people are sick, and a test is 99% accurate, a positive test does not mean 99% chance of being sick - Bayes adjusts it.

Like a detective updating the suspect list each time a new clue arrives.

Conditional Probability
Probability

Algebra of true/false values. The math behind computer logic gates and binary operations.

true AND false = false. true OR false = true. NOT true = false.

Like light switches - two switches in series (AND) need both on; in parallel (OR) need at least one on.

Logic
Set Theory

The math of continuous change. Derivatives measure change; integrals accumulate it.

Calculus lets us compute how loss changes as weights change, which is how neural networks learn.
🔗 Analogy
Like the math of motion - derivatives are speed (instant change), integrals are distance (total accumulation).

Derivative
Gradient

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/chain-rule.title: chain-rule
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/chain-rule.content:
Chain Rule

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Lets us compute derivatives of composite functions. Essential for backpropagation in neural networks.
📋 Concrete Example
If y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f-prime(g(x)) times g-prime(x). This is how backprop propagates gradients layer by layer.
🔗 Analogy
Like tracking a rumor through a chain of friends - each person changes it a bit, and you multiply all the changes.
Related Concepts

Derivative
Backpropagation
Function Composition

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/conditional.title: conditional-probability
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/conditional.content:
Conditional Probability

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
The probability of an event given that another event has already happened.
📋 Concrete Example
P(rain | dark clouds) is much higher than P(rain) in general. Knowing clouds change the odds.
🔗 Analogy
Like the probability your bus is late changes once you hear there was an accident on the road.
Related Concepts

Probability
Bayes Theorem

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/convex-func.title: convex-function
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/convex-func.content:
Convex Function

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
A bowl-shaped function with one global minimum. Easy to optimize - any downhill path reaches the bottom.
📋 Concrete Example
f(x) = x squared is convex. Gradient descent always finds the bottom, no matter where you start.
🔗 Analogy
Like a smooth bowl - a marble rolled from anywhere will settle at the lowest point.
Related Concepts

Optimization
Global Minimum
Local Minimum

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/correlation.title: correlation
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/correlation.content:
Correlation

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Measures how two variables move together. Correlation is not causation.
📋 Concrete Example
Ice cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer - correlated, but ice cream does not cause drowning.
🔗 Analogy
Like two dancers moving together - they might be following the same music, not one leading the other.
Related Concepts

Statistics
Covariance

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/cosine-simi.title: cosine-similarity
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/cosine-simi.content:
Cosine Similarity

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Measures the angle between two vectors, ignoring their length. Great for comparing meaning.
📋 Concrete Example
Vectors for king and queen have a small angle (high cosine similarity, about 0.7). King and banana have a large angle.
🔗 Analogy
Like comparing the direction two people are walking - same direction means similar, regardless of speed.
Related Concepts

Dot Product
Vector
Embedding

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/covariance.title: covariance
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/covariance.content:
Covariance

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Measures how two variables change together. Positive means they rise together; negative means one rises as the other falls.
📋 Concrete Example
Study hours and grades have positive covariance. TV hours and grades might have negative covariance.
🔗 Analogy
Like two friends on a seesaw - if one goes up while the other goes down, that is negative covariance.
Related Concepts

Correlation
Variance
Statistics

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/cross-entro.title: cross-entropy
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/cross-entro.content:
Cross-Entropy

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Measures the difference between two probability distributions. Used as a loss function in classification.
📋 Concrete Example
If the true label is cat but the model predicts only 10% cat, cross-entropy loss is high. If 90%, it is low.
🔗 Analogy
Like a penalty for being wrong and confident - you lose points for assigning low probability to the truth.
Related Concepts

Entropy
Loss Function
Softmax
KL Divergence

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/derivative.title: derivative
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/derivative.content:
Derivative

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Measures how fast a function changes at a point. The slope of the tangent line.
📋 Concrete Example
For f(x) = x squared, the derivative is 2x. At x=3, slope is 6.
🔗 Analogy
Like a speedometer showing how fast your position changes at this instant.
Related Concepts

Gradient
Chain Rule
Calculus

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/dimension.title: dimension
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/dimension.content:
Dimension

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
The number of independent directions in a space. Each feature adds a dimension.
📋 Concrete Example
A 3-feature dataset (height, weight, age) is 3-dimensional. An image with 784 pixels is 784-dimensional.
🔗 Analogy
Like the axes on a graph - 2 axes is a flat plane, 3 axes is a 3D space, more axes are beyond what we can picture.
Related Concepts

Vector
Dimensionality Reduction
PCA

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/dot-product.title: dot-product
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/dot-product.content:
Dot Product

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Multiplies two vectors element-wise and sums the result. Measures how aligned two vectors are.
📋 Concrete Example
Dot of [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6] = 14 + 25 + 3*6 = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32.
🔗 Analogy
Like two people pulling a cart - if they pull in the same direction, their effort adds up; if opposite, it cancels.
Related Concepts

Vector
Matrix Multiplication
Cosine Similarity

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/eigenvalue-.title: eigenvalue-eigenvector
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/eigenvalue-.content:
Eigenvalue Eigenvector

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Special vectors that only stretch or shrink under a transformation (eigenvectors), by a factor (eigenvalues).
📋 Concrete Example
PCA finds eigenvectors of the covariance matrix. The largest eigenvalues mark the most important directions.
🔗 Analogy
Like finding the natural grain of a piece of wood - along the grain (eigenvector) it stretches evenly, by the eigenvalue amount.
Related Concepts

PCA
Linear Algebra
Matrix

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/entropy.title: entropy
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/entropy.content:
Entropy

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Measures uncertainty or randomness. Higher entropy means more chaos, less predictability.
📋 Concrete Example
A fair coin has entropy of 1 bit. A loaded coin with 99% heads has much lower entropy.
🔗 Analogy
Like the messiness of a bedroom - a tidy room (predictable) has low entropy, a chaotic one has high.
Related Concepts

Cross-Entropy
KL Divergence
Information Theory

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/euclidean-d.title: euclidean-distance
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/euclidean-d.content:
Euclidean Distance

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
The straight-line distance between two points. Used to measure similarity in feature space.
📋 Concrete Example
Distance between [0,0] and [3,4] = square root of (9+16) = 5.
🔗 Analogy
Like measuring with a ruler between two dots on a map - the direct straight line.
Related Concepts

Hypotenuse
Vector
Cosine Similarity

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/expected-va.title: expected-value
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/expected-va.content:
Expected Value

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
The long-run average of a random variable. What you would expect on average over many trials.
📋 Concrete Example
Rolling a fair 6-sided die: expected value = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5. You won’t roll 3.5, but over many rolls the average approaches it.
🔗 Analogy
Like the average score you would get playing a game many, many times - not any single game’s score.
Related Concepts

Mean
Probability
Statistics

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/exponent.title: exponent
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/exponent.content:
Exponent

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Repeated multiplication. The inverse of logarithm. Growth can be explosive.
📋 Concrete Example
2 to the power 10 = 1024. Exponential growth doubles each step: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, …
🔗 Analogy
Like a rumor spreading where each person tells 2 new people - the numbers explode quickly.
Related Concepts

Logarithm
Exponential Growth
Sigmoid

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/exponential.title: exponential-growth
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/exponential.content:
Exponential Growth

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Growth that multiplies by a constant each step, not adds. How things go viral.
📋 Concrete Example
If followers double each day: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16… After 20 days, over 1 million.
🔗 Analogy
Like a chain letter - each person who gets it sends it to more, and the numbers explode.
Related Concepts

Exponent
Logarithm

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/function-co.title: function-composition
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/function-co.content:
Function Composition

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Applying one function after another. Neural networks are deep compositions of simple functions.
📋 Concrete Example
If f(x) = x+1 and g(x) = x*2, then g(f(x)) = (x+1)*2. A 10-layer network composes 10 functions.
🔗 Analogy
Like a series of filters on a photo app - each filter feeds into the next, building the final image.
Related Concepts

Chain Rule
Neural Network
Forward Pass

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/global-mini.title: global-minimum
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/global-mini.content:
Global Minimum

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
The absolute lowest point of the function. The goal of optimization.
📋 Concrete Example
For f(x) = x squared, the global minimum is at x=0, f(x)=0.
🔗 Analogy
Like the deepest point in the ocean - the true bottom, not just a local trench.
Related Concepts

Local Minimum
Convex Function
Optimization

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/gradient.title: gradient
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/gradient.content:
Gradient

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
A vector pointing in the direction of steepest increase. Negative gradient points toward decrease.
📋 Concrete Example
On a hill, the gradient points uphill. To descend, you go in the opposite direction.
🔗 Analogy
Like a compass that always points to the steepest way up a mountain; flip it to find the way down.
Related Concepts

Derivative
Gradient Descent
Partial Derivative

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/hypotenuse.title: hypotenuse
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/hypotenuse.content:
Hypotenuse

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
The longest side of a right triangle, opposite the right angle. Foundation of distance calculations.
📋 Concrete Example
For sides 3 and 4, the hypotenuse is 5 (Pythagorean theorem: 3 squared + 4 squared = 5 squared).
🔗 Analogy
Like the shortcut across a rectangular field - longer than either side, but the direct route.
Related Concepts

Euclidean Distance
Vector

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/identity-ma.title: identity-matrix
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/identity-ma.content:
Identity Matrix

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
A matrix with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere. Multiplying by it changes nothing.
📋 Concrete Example
The 3x3 identity is [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]]. Any matrix times identity equals itself.
🔗 Analogy
Like multiplying a number by 1 - the value stays exactly the same.
Related Concepts

Matrix
Matrix Multiplication

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/independent.title: independent-events
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/independent.content:
Independent Events

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Two events are independent if one happening does not change the probability of the other.
📋 Concrete Example
Coin flips are independent - getting heads on flip 1 does not change the odds for flip 2.
🔗 Analogy
Like two friends flipping coins separately - neither result affects the other.
Related Concepts

Conditional Probability
Probability

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/information.title: information-theory
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/information.content:
Information Theory

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
The study of quantifying information, uncertainty, and communication. Foundation of modern ML loss functions.
📋 Concrete Example
Shannon entropy measures the average bits needed to encode messages from a source.
🔗 Analogy
Like a postal pricing system - it costs more bits to send surprising news than predictable news.
Related Concepts

Entropy
Cross-Entropy
KL Divergence

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/inverse-mat.title: inverse-matrix
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/inverse-mat.content:
Inverse Matrix

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
A matrix that undoes another matrix. Multiplying them gives the identity matrix.
📋 Concrete Example
If A times B = identity, then B is the inverse of A. Used to solve linear systems.
🔗 Analogy
Like an undo button - apply matrix A, then its inverse, and you are back where you started.
Related Concepts

Matrix
Identity Matrix

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/kl-divergen.title: kl-divergence
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/kl-divergen.content:
KL Divergence

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Measures how one probability distribution differs from another. Not symmetric - direction matters.
📋 Concrete Example
Compare a predicted word distribution to the true one. KL divergence quantifies the gap.
🔗 Analogy
Like measuring how different your map is from the real city layout - useful for knowing how much to correct.
Related Concepts

Entropy
Cross-Entropy
Information Theory

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/linear-alge.title: linear-algebra
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/linear-alge.content:
Linear Algebra

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
The study of vectors, matrices, and linear transformations. The language of data in AI.
📋 Concrete Example
Representing 1 million images as a matrix and multiplying by a weight matrix to classify them.
🔗 Analogy
Like the grammar of multi-dimensional space - it lets us describe and manipulate data efficiently.
Related Concepts

Vector
Matrix
Eigenvalue Eigenvector

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/linear-mode.title: linear-model
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/linear-mode.content:
Linear Model

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
The simplest model: output is a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias. A straight-line or flat-plane relationship.
📋 Concrete Example
Predict house price = 10000area + 5000rooms - 1000*age + 50000. A linear combination of features.
🔗 Analogy
Like a recipe: a fixed amount of each ingredient gives the result. No complex interactions.

Logistic Regression
Regression
Weights

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/linear-sepa.title: linear-separability
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/linear-sepa.content:
Linear Separability

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
When classes can be separated by a straight line (or flat plane). Simple models can handle this; complex data needs more.
📋 Concrete Example
Cats vs dogs on a height-weight graph might be separable by a line. Cats vs dogs photos cannot.
🔗 Analogy
Like sorting coins by drawing a line - easy if they are clearly separated, impossible if mixed.
Related Concepts

Linear Model
Classification
Perceptron

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/local-minim.title: local-minimum
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/local-minim.content:
Local Minimum

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
A low point that is not the lowest overall. Gradient descent can get stuck here.
📋 Concrete Example
On a bumpy loss surface, the gradient might lead to a small valley that is not the deepest point.
🔗 Analogy
Like resting in a small ditch on a mountainside - you are low locally, but not at the valley floor.
Related Concepts

Global Minimum
Convex Function
Gradient Descent

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/logarithm.title: logarithm
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/logarithm.content:
Logarithm

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
The inverse of exponentiation. Compresses huge ranges into manageable numbers. Used in loss functions and probabilities.
📋 Concrete Example
log base 10 of 1000 = 3, because 10 to the power 3 = 1000. log turns multiplication into addition.
🔗 Analogy
Like a zoom lens that shrinks vast distances so you can see them on one map.
Related Concepts

Exponent
Entropy
Cross-Entropy

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/logic.title: logic
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/logic.content:
Logic

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
The formal rules of reasoning. AND, OR, NOT combine statements to reach conclusions.
📋 Concrete Example
If it is raining AND I have an umbrella, then I go out. If NOT raining, I go out without one.
🔗 Analogy
Like the rules of a board game - clear yes/no decisions that combine to determine the outcome.
Related Concepts

Set Theory
Boolean Algebra

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/logistic-re.title: logistic-regression
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/logistic-re.content:
Logistic Regression

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
A simple classification model using sigmoid to predict probabilities. The building block before neural networks.
📋 Concrete Example
Predict whether a student passes (1) or fails (0) based on study hours, using a sigmoid on a linear combination.
🔗 Analogy
Like a bouncer with a sliding scale - the more study hours you have, the higher your chance of getting in.
Related Concepts

Sigmoid
Classification
Linear Model

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/matrix-mult.title: matrix-multiplication
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/matrix-mult.content:
Matrix Multiplication

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Combines two matrices to produce a new one. The core operation in every neural network layer.
📋 Concrete Example
A 3x2 matrix times a 2x4 matrix gives a 3x4 matrix. Each output cell is a dot product of a row and column.
🔗 Analogy
Like a factory assembly line where each station combines parts from two supply lines to make a new product.

Matrix
Dot Product
Forward Pass

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/matrix-tran.title: matrix-transpose
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/matrix-tran.content:
Matrix Transpose

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
Flips a matrix over its diagonal, swapping rows and columns. Used everywhere in ML computations.
📋 Concrete Example
Transpose of [[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]] (3x2) becomes [[1,3,5],[2,4,6]] (2x3).

Like turning a photo sideways - rows become columns and columns become rows.

Matrix
Matrix Multiplication

agentic-coding/08-math-logic/matrix.title: matrix
agentic-coding/08-math-logic/matrix.content:
Matrix

Domain: Math & Logic for AI

🎯 Motivation
A grid of numbers. Used to store data and perform many calculations at once.
📋 Concrete Example
A class of 30 students each with 5 subject scores is a 30-row by 5-column matrix.
🔗 Analogy
Like a spreadsheet - rows are students, columns are subjects, each cell holds a number.
